case_name: CASE OF GALINA ROŞCA AND OTHERS v. THE REPUBLIC OF MOLDOVA
full_case_text_no_verdict:
FIFTH SECTION

CASE OF GALINA ROŞCA AND OTHERS v. THE REPUBLIC OF MOLDOVA

(Application no. 14975/15)











JUDGMENT


STRASBOURG

24 September 2026





This judgment is final but it may be subject to editorial revision.





In the case of Galina Roşca and Others v. the Republic of Moldova,

The European Court of Human Rights (Fifth Section), sitting as a Committee composed of:

Andreas Zünd, President,
Mykola Gnatovskyy,
Vahe Grigoryan, judges,
and Martina Keller, Deputy Section Registrar,

Having regard to:

the application (no. 14975/15) against the Republic of Moldova lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) on 14 March 2015 by three Moldovan nationals, relevant details listed in the appended table, (“the applicants”) who were represented by Mr M. Belinschi, a lawyer practising in Chişinău;

the decision to give notice of the complaints concerning a breach of the principle of legal certainty to the Moldovan Government (“the Government”), represented by their Agent, Mr D. Obadă, and to declare inadmissible the remainder of the application;

the parties’ observations;

Having deliberated in private on 3 September 2026,

Delivers the following judgment, which was adopted on that date:

SUBJECT MATTER OF THE CASE

1.  The case concerns an alleged breach of the principle of “legal certainty”. The applicants complained under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention and under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention.

2.  A certain R.P. had four children: R.I, R.T., R.G and R.Gr. In April 2000 R.P. died. He left a will whereby he bequeathed certain property (plots of land, hereinafter “the testate property”) to R.I. On an unknown date within six months of R.P.’s death, R.I. formally accepted the succession under the will and on 8 November 2000 was issued with a certificate attesting his right as heir to the testate property.

3.  The first applicant was married to R.G. until his death on an unspecified date before R.P.’s death. The second and third applicants are the children of R.G. and the first applicant. Prior to R.P.’s death the applicants had lived on his property. They continued to do so after his death.

first set of proceedings

4.  In February 2011 R.I., represented by G.A., obtained from the notary public in charge of R.P.’s succession proceedings a certificate attesting to his right to a part of the property not covered by the will. He then donated that property to G.V. On 29 March 2011 G.V. brought court proceedings seeking the applicants’ removal from the disputed property. On 30 March 2011 the applicants lodged a counter-claim which was aimed at annulling a certificate attesting that R.I. was the heir to the part of the property not covered by the will and the donation of that property to G.V., as well as the formal recognition that they had de facto accepted R.P.’s succession by living on the property.

5.  On 15 November 2011 the Criuleni District Court accepted G.V.’s claims and rejected those lodged by the applicants. The court found that R.I. had accepted the succession within six months, as required by law. Moreover, since R.G. was already dead at the time of R.P.’s death, the applicants did not have a right to the property as his heirs under the law.

6.  On 15 May 2012 the Chișinău Court of Appeal overturned that judgment and accepted the applicants’ claims. It found that under the law the applicants had risen to the rank which R.G. would have attained if he were alive at the time of R.P.’s death. The court decided that after R.P.’s death, the applicants had de facto accepted the succession by living on his property. It also established that none of R.P.’s other children, including R.I., had accepted R.P.’s succession of the property not covered by the will within six months of his death. Moreover, R.I. had not only missed the six-month time-limit for accepting the succession, but when he had eventually done so in February 2011, he had not acted personally but via a representative (G.A.), which was contrary to the law. The court ultimately found that R.I. “did not have the legal or moral right to [the disputed property]”.

7.  R.I. and G.V. lodged an appeal on points of law, arguing, inter alia, that when R.I. had accepted the succession within six months of R.P.’s death, he had done so in respect of the entire property that he could inherit, both the property bequeathed in the will and his part of the remainder of property. They also argued that while the Court of Appeal had established the applicants’ de facto acceptance of the succession, it did not take into account that R.I. had also formally accepted the succession within six months as required by law. Lastly, they argued that under the applicable law, when an heir accepted a succession, he or she did so with respect to the entirety of the estate, which implied that by accepting the succession of the testate property, R.I. had also accepted the succession of his share of the property not covered by the will.

8.  On 2 January 2013 the Supreme Court of Justice upheld the lower court’s judgment. It found, inter alia, that in 2000 R.I. had only requested a certificate attesting that he was the heir based on the will, and not a certificate of intestate inheritance, which he had requested only in 2011. On 30 April 2014 the same court rejected an extraordinary appeal lodged by R.Gr., who complained about not being involved in the proceedings and that the higher courts had not reacted to the viewing in court of the notarised declarations by two of R.P.’s nieces and nephews (including one of the applicants, Ms Roșca Diana), according to which they had refused to inherit R.P.’s property.

second set of proceedings

9.  On 27 May 2013 the applicants brought court proceedings against the notary public in charge of R.P.’s succession proceedings, asking to have the certificate attesting that Roșca Andrei (the second applicant) was the heir to one quarter of the part of R.P.’s property not covered by his will annulled and that it be replaced by other certificates according to which each of the three applicants had the right to one third of that property.

10.  On 11 December 2013 the Criuleni District Court accepted the applicants’ claims, finding that the facts established in a final court decision did not have to be proved again and could not be contested in subsequent court proceedings.

11.  On 30 July 2014 the Chișinău Court of Appeal set aside that decision and adopted another one, rejecting the applicants’ claims. It found that although the judgment of 15 May 2012 had become final (see paragraph 6 above), it had only established that the applicants had the right to inherit, but not that they were the only heirs. Since R.I. had also accepted the succession within six months of R.P.’s death, he had the right to obtain a part of the property not covered by R.P.’s will.

12.  The applicants appealed, arguing, inter alia, that the Court of Appeal had not properly taken into account the judgment of 15 May 2012, which had established that R.I. did not have the right to the disputed property. On 3 December 2014 the Supreme Court of Justice rejected the appeal as unfounded.
target_provision: Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (Protection of property)
target_question: whether the Court finds a violation by the Republic of Moldova of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (Protection of property) concerning Peaceful enjoyment of possessions in this case

case_name: CASE OF M.C. v. HUNGARY
full_case_text_no_verdict:
FIFTH SECTION

CASE OF M.C. v. HUNGARY

(Application no. 32317/23)













JUDGMENT


STRASBOURG

1 October 2026







This judgment is final but it may be subject to editorial revision.



In the case of M.C. v. Hungary,

The European Court of Human Rights (Fifth Section), sitting as a Committee composed of:

María Elósegui, President,
Gilberto Felici,
Diana Sârcu, judges,
and Sophie Piquet, Acting Deputy Section Registrar,

Having regard to:

the application (no. 32317/23) against Hungary lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) on 24 July 2023 by a Serbian national, Mr M.C. (“the applicant”), who was born in 1978 and lived in Jászapáti at the material time, and was represented by Ms E. Kadlót, a lawyer practising in Budapest;

the decision to give notice of the complaints concerning Articles 8 and 13 of the Convention to the Hungarian Government (“the Government”), represented by their Agent, Mr Z. Tallódi, of the Ministry of Justice, and to declare the remainder of the application inadmissible;

the decision not to disclose the applicant’s name;

the parties’ observations;

the decision of the Serbian Government not to exercise its right to intervene in the proceedings (Article 36 § 1 of the Convention);



Having deliberated in private on 10 September 2026,

Delivers the following judgment, which was adopted on that date:

SUBJECT MATTER OF THE CASE

1.  The application concerns whether the dismissal of the applicant’s request for the renewal of his residence permit for employment purposes on grounds of national security and his simultaneous expulsion from Hungary to Serbia were attended by sufficient procedural safeguards as required under Article 8 of the Convention.

2.  The applicant is a Serbian national who had been residing in Hungary since 2010 for employment purposes.

3.  On 22 February 2022 the applicant lodged a request for a residence permit for the purposes of employment.

4.  On 25 April 2022 the National Directorate-General for Aliens Policing (hereinafter “NDGAP”) dismissed his application on the ground that the applicant’s residence posed a threat to public safety of Hungary on the basis of the opinion of the Jász-Nagykun-Szolnok police department. Following an appeal by the applicant, on 7 July 2022 the NDGAP, acting at second instance, quashed the first-instance decision, finding that, on the basis of a police opinion obtained in the appeal proceedings, the applicant did not constitute a risk, and remitted the case.

5.  On 13 October 2022, in the resumed proceedings, the NDGAP dismissed the applicant’s application and expelled him to Serbia. It held in its decision that the conditions of a residence permit, in particular with regard to the applicant’s employment, housing, sufficient means to sustain his residence and health insurance, had been met. Nonetheless, the Constitution Protection Office (Alkotmányvédelmi Hivatal – hereinafter “the CPO”) established, in its opinion of 27 September 2022, that the applicant posed a threat to national security. The NDGAP therefore dismissed the applicant’s request on the basis of the relevant provisions of sections 13(1)(h) and 18(1)(a) of Act no. II of 2007 on the admission and right of residence of third‑country nationals (hereinafter “the Immigration Act”). The underlying information contained in the CPO’s assessment was classified, in accordance with Act no. CLV of 2009 on the protection of classified information (hereinafter “the Classified Information Act”).

6.  The applicant lodged an appeal against that decision. In the appeal proceedings, the CPO maintained its findings concerning the national security risk. Relying on that assessment, the NDGAP, acting at second instance, emphasised that, given the CPO’s opinion, the consideration of any other conditions was excluded.

7.  Subsequently, the applicant sought judicial review. On 5 April 2023 the Debrecen High Court dismissed his action. It held, in so far as relevant, that the NDGAP was not bound by the CPO’s assessment. Nevertheless, for want of any circumstances that might have suggested otherwise, it based its decision exclusively on that. At the same time, it explained that there was no opportunity for the consideration of the applicant’s personal circumstances, given that in the event of the existence of a national security risk, the rejection of the residence permit request was compulsory. In this regard it noted that such national security risk had been established by the CPO. The trial judge consulted the classified documents and confirmed the CPO’s assessment.

8.  On 20 June 2023 the Kúria declared the applicant’s petition for judicial review inadmissible. The applicant did not lodge a constitutional complaint with the Constitutional Court.

9.  In the meantime, the applicant requested access to the CPO’s classified report under the Classified Information Act. Nevertheless, on 11 November 2022 the CPO rejected his application. It appears that his request for judicial review was to no avail.

10.  The relevant domestic and EU law and practice have been set out in Trapitsyna and Isaeva v. Hungary (no. 5488/22, §§ 25‑36, 19 September 2024), and Demirci v. Hungary (no. 48302/21, §§ 21‑23, 6 May 2025).

11.  In addition, in accordance with section 13(1)(h) of the Immigration Act, a third-country national may enter Hungary for a stay exceeding 90 days within a period of 180 days, and may stay in Hungary for a period exceeding 90 days within a period of 180 days, if his or her entry or stay does not pose a danger to national security in Hungary. Furthermore, as per section 18(1)(a), failure to meet the above condition will lead to the refusal of the issuance or extension of a residence permit or the revoking of an issued residence permit.

12.  In constitutional complaint proceedings in unrelated cases, the Constitutional Court found that the question whether the concerned individual’s presence in Hungary had constituted a threat to national security could not be reassessed as part of constitutional proceedings, since this would have amounted to a re-examination of the facts (see decision no. 3439/2021. (X. 25.) AB of 5 October 2021 in Trapitsyna and Isaeva, cited above, § 18). It considered that that task pertained to the ordinary court’s competence (see decision no. 3457/2021. (XI. 3.) AB of 19 October 2021; decision no. 3438/2021. (X. 25.) AB of 5 October 2021; and decision no. 3440/2021. (X. 25.) AB of 5 October 2021).

13.  Furthermore, the Constitutional Court held that it could not review the matter of access to classified information and the related procedural questions, as those had not been subject to the immigration proceedings concerned by the constitutional complaint (see decision no. 3440/2021. (X. 25.) AB of 5 October 2021, and decision no. 3417/2020. (XI. 26.) AB of 10 November 2020).

14.  The applicant complained under Article 8 of the Convention that for want of any connection with his country of origin, his expulsion had violated his right to respect for his private life. He further complained that he had been expelled without being afforded sufficient procedural guarantees. Relying on Article 13 of the Convention, he submitted that, without access to the grounds of the alleged national security risk, he had had no effective remedy against the expulsion decision.

target_issue: Expulsion; Article 8-1 - Respect for private life

case_name: CASE OF ANAR MAMMADOV v. AZERBAIJAN
full_case_text_no_verdict:
THIRD SECTION

CASE OF ANAR MAMMADOV v. AZERBAIJAN

(Applications nos. 12043/19 and 50484/20)





JUDGMENTSTRASBOURG

6 October 2026



This judgment will become final in the circumstances set out in Article 44 § 2 of the Convention. It may be subject to editorial revision.

In the case of Anar Mammadov v. Azerbaijan,

The European Court of Human Rights (Third Section), sitting as a Chamber composed of:

Ioannis Ktistakis, President,
Lətif Hüseynov,
Darian Pavli,
Úna Ní Raifeartaigh,
Mateja Đurović,
Canòlic Mingorance Cairat,
Vasilka Sancin, judges,
and Milan Blaško, Section Registrar,

Having regard to:

the applications nos. 12043/19 and 50484/20 against the Republic of Azerbaijan lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by an Azerbaijani national, Mr Anar Shahin oglu Mammadov (Anar Şahin oğlu Məmmədov - the applicant), on 19 February 2019 and 23 October 2020 respectively;

the decision to give notice to the Azerbaijani Government (“the Government”) of the complaints under Articles 8, 10, 13 and 18 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention and to declare the remainder of the applications inadmissible;

the parties’ observations;

Having deliberated in private on 8 September 2026,

Delivers the following judgment, which was adopted on that date:

INTRODUCTION

1.  The present case concerns criminal proceedings brought against the applicant, a journalist, and a seizure operation carried out in his flat within the framework of those criminal proceedings. The applicant raised various complaints under Articles 8, 10, 13 and 18 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention.

THE FACTS

2.  The applicant was born in 1979 and lives in Baku. He was represented by Mr E. Sadigov, a lawyer based in Baku.

3.  The Government were represented by their Agent, Mr Ç. Əsgərov.

4.  The facts of the case may be summarised as follows.

background information

5.  The applicant is a journalist and the chief editor of the news website criminal.az.

6.  He had previously been formally warned by the prosecuting authorities in 2015 and 2017 for various articles he had published on the website, which were alleged to contain false and biased information. There is no information in the case file to suggest that the applicant challenged those warnings in the domestic courts at that time.

7.  On 3 July 2018 an assassination attempt was made on the head of the Ganja City Executive Authority (“GCEA”), E.V., leaving him and his bodyguard seriously injured. The incident was followed by riots in Ganja during which two police officers were killed.

8.  Between 3 and 5 July 2018, the applicant published several articles discussing the possible causes of the assassination attempt. Two of these articles, which later formed the basis of the charges against him, were entitled “Scandalous and troublesome journey of shot head of Ganja – behind the scenes with the headbutting General [R.M.]” (Gəncənin güllənənən başçısının qalmaqallı və bəlalı yolu – General [R.M.] ilə kəllələşmənin pərdəarxası), and “‘The Ganja events follow [E.V.]’s rudeness’” (‘Gəncədə baş verən hadisə [E.V.]-in kobudluğunun nəticəsidir’).

9.  The first article started with the information that criminal.az had obtained a passport photograph of Y.S., the person who had made the assassination attempt. The article continued:

“Why E.V. was shot remains unclear. One possibility is that a conflict had arisen between Y.S. and the head of the GCEA. According to some accounts, Y.S. had even warned the head [of the GCEA] that he would kill him.

Those who have known [E.V.] since his appointment in 2011 as the head of Ganja will know that E.V. sought to bring all state institutions in the city under his control. Although the police answered to the Minister of Internal Affairs and the prosecutor to the Prosecutor General, E.V. allegedly compelled them to obey him. This led to a serious conflict between the late Ganja police chief, Major General R.M., and the head [of the GCEA]. While R.M. was the police chief in Ganja, a dispute arose between him and E.V. concerning the mother of a martyr [a soldier who had fallen during the war in Karabakh].

There were rumours that, during an official event, the mother of a martyr had approached E.V. and reproached him for the demolition of her house. E.V. had allegedly ordered the police to arrest her. Later in a meeting, he reportedly used rude language towards R.M., who had shown sympathy toward the mother. At one point, E.V. and R.M. even came to blows. Afterwards, R.M. left Ganja. ... Two years later, he died in Baku. ...

There were even rumours circulating that R.M. had been shot in his official car by individuals allegedly close to E.V.”

10.  The article further referred to a blog by a political analyst and alleged that E.V. was being considered for the position of head of Baku [City Executive Authority]. The quoted blog stated that E.V. had “done his best to destroy everything from the architecture of Ganja to its very soul”.

11.  The article further recounted that E.V. was not the first head of the GCEA who had been shot, noting that in 1993 the then‑head of Ganja, H.V., had been killed after a violent confrontation with a criminal figure. The article concluded by noting that E.V. was the brother of K.V., the military prosecutor of the Republic of Azerbaijan.

12.  In the second article, the applicant quoted another media outlet extensively, starting with a quotation that said: “‘The authorities do not want to see that the population of the country’s second‑largest city is dissatisfied with the arbitrariness” (“Hakimiyyət ikinci böyük şəhərin əhalisinin özbaşınalıqdan narazı olduğunu görmək istəmir”).

13.  The article further continued:

“‘The country’s leadership is attempting to downplay yesterday’s assassination attempt on the head of the Ganja City Executive Authority, E.V., as a mere criminal incident’. This is stated in the material of the Turan news agency.

... According to the author of the article, the authorities either do not want to see, or are deliberately ignoring, the fact that the population of Ganja ... is dissatisfied with the rudeness and arbitrariness of the city’s leadership. ‘The proud and courageous people of Ganja have long been unhappy with E.V. He openly insults people, violates their property rights, and humiliates their honour and dignity. Such behaviour is in sharp contradiction to the rules set by the head of state. The President has repeatedly called on state officials to treat citizens’ rights with respect and has said that those who behave rudely and irresponsibly would be punished.

Why does [I.A.] [the president] not see E.V.’s arbitrariness and rudeness, why does he not punish him? Or does I.A. say these things only for form’s sake?’ residents of Ganja complain, so the article states. One resident, who wished to remain anonymous, said that the reason for the assassination attempt on E.V. was his rude treatment of citizens. ‘Some time ago, one of the local residents approached him regarding her problem. E.V. shouted, cursed, and expelled the woman, who was pregnant, from the office. The person who opened fire at E.V. ... is that woman’s brother. The people of Ganja have always been proud and fearless. Therefore, what happened to E.V. was bound to occur sooner or later. If the authorities do not draw conclusions from this, the events of Ismayilli and Quba [riots by locals who were dissatisfied with the rude behaviour of the officials] may be repeated in Ganja’; the article says.”

14.  The article continued quoting a former official of the Ministry of National Security, who stated that E.V. had been shot because of his inappropriate behaviour towards the population. It concluded with a brief description of the assassination attempt.

Seizure of the applicant’s BELONGINGS, and the related court proceedings

15.  On 9 July 2018 the Prosecutor General’s Office published a press statement about the above-mentioned assassination attempt. It stated, inter alia, that certain officials from various media sources and other individuals had spread false and provocative information online in connection with a “premeditated act of terror” on 3 July 2018. The online publications in question had included false information and information the dissemination of which was prohibited by law and which incited terrorism, the forcible seizure of power and the forcible change of the constitutional order, with the aim of confusing public opinion, breaching public and political order and casting a bad light over the measures taken by law-enforcement authorities in the fight against crime. The prosecuting authorities had instituted criminal proceedings under Articles 214-2 (public incitement to terrorism) and 281.1 (public call against the State) of the Criminal Code and were taking steps to identify the perpetrators. In addition, despite officials from the internet information resources criminal.az and bastainfo.com having recently being given two warnings by the Prosecutor General’s Office for breaching the requirements of the mass media legislation, the two websites had again breached those legal requirements by publishing, between 3 and 6 July 2018, various articles containing false and prohibited information aimed at confusing the public, breaching public order and causing citizens to distrust measures taken by the State. Criminal proceedings had been instituted under Article 313 (forgery by an official) of the Criminal Code. In addition, officials from the above‑mentioned two websites, as well as from topxeber.az and fia.az, had been called to the Prosecutor General’s Office and again given formal warnings. The Prosecutor General’s Office had also asked the Ministry of Transport, Communication and High Technologies (“the MTCHT”) to block access to the four websites.

16.  On 9 July 2018 the applicant was called in for questioning by the Baku City Prosecutor’s Office, where he was questioned for several hours about the above-mentioned articles without a lawyer being present.

17.  The applicant claimed that as soon as the questioning started the investigators seized his two mobile telephones and examined them although they did not have a court order authorising them to do so. After the questioning, the applicant was required to write out and sign a statement (ərizə) which was dictated to him and which read as follows:

“I do not object to voluntarily handing over the two mobile telephones that I use (istifadəmdə olan iki ədəd mobil telefon cihazını), two laptops that [we] use at home (evimdə istifadə etdiyimiz 2 ədəd kompyuteri), and documents related to the criminal.az website to the investigation in order to clarify the truth in the criminal proceedings instituted under Article 313 of the Criminal Code by the Investigation Unit of the Baku City Prosecutor’s Office.

It has been explained to me that the seized items will be returned to me after matters are resolved.”

18.  On the same day the investigator issued a decision on seizure (götürmə haqqında qərar). In it he relied on Article 243.3 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (the CCrP) and stated that on the ground of the concealment, in a residence, of items or documents indicating the commission of a crime against a person or the State authority, the two mobile telephones, two laptops and certain documents were to be seized from the applicant.

19.  After the questioning on 9 July 2018, the applicant was accompanied to his flat by the investigator, where the seizure operation was carried out in the presence of the applicant and two attesting witnesses. A laptop and documents belonging to Criminal.az LLC (a bank statement, the company’s certificate of state registration, and its charter) were seized. The investigators also inspected a laptop which belonged to the applicant’s wife. No court order authorising the seizure operation was provided by the investigators.

20.  After the seizure had been carried out, a seizure record (götürülmə aparılması haqqında protokol) was issued by the investigator on the same date. It stated in pre-printed text, inter alia, that a seizure operation had been carried out in the applicant’s flat in accordance with the requirements of Articles 85, 242-245 and 247 of the CCrP. The record also contained pre‑printed text saying that the applicant (his name had been added in handwriting) had been invited to hand the items over voluntarily and that he had agreed to do so. The record was signed by the attesting witnesses and the investigator and by the applicant, who acknowledged in it that he had received a copy of the record. However, he later stated that he had in fact not been provided with a copy of the record.

21.  Assuming that there had been a court decision permitting the seizure operation that had been carried out, on 11 July 2018 the applicant lodged two separate appeals with the Baku Court of Appeal, both of which had the same wording. In those appeals, the applicant changed only the name of the first‑instance court because he did not know exactly which first-instance court, the Sabail District Court or the Sabunchu District Court, had authorised the seizure operation. He claimed that the prosecuting authorities had conducted a seizure operation at his flat and seized various items and inspected their contents without any legal basis and without having charged him with any offence, in violation of his right to respect for his home and private life. The applicant claimed that those actions had been aimed at collecting evidence to bring additional charges against him in the future, as there was no connection between the criminal proceedings initiated under Article 313 of the Criminal Code and the seizure operation carried out at his flat. He asked the appellate court, inter alia, to quash the Sabail District Court’s and Sabunchu District Court’s decisions authorising the seizure, to declare them unlawful, and to order the return of the seized items.

22.  Following an inquiry by the appellate court, it became clear that the Sabunchu District Court had not issued any decision authorising the seizure. The appellate court returned the applicant’s appeal without considering it, stating that to be the case.

23.  On 18 July 2018 the applicant applied to the Prosecutor General’s Office asking for the return of the seized items. He also requested information about his procedural status – whether he had been considered a witness or a suspect – during the questioning conducted on 9 July 2018.

24.  By a letter of 24 August 2018, the Prosecutor General’s Office responded to the applicant that he “had been questioned, initially without representation, later with the participation of his representative because of the needs of the investigation”, and that “it will be ensured that a lawful decision is issued in respect of the seized items”.

25.  On 23 July 2018 the applicant lodged a complaint against the investigator of the Baku City Prosecutor’s Office with the Sabail District Court under the judicial supervision procedure under Article 449 (procedure for the review of the lawfulness of procedural actions or decisions by the prosecuting authorities) of the CCrP. He asked the court to declare the seizure operation conducted in his flat unlawful, to order the return of the seized items and to find that certain of his rights under the Convention had been violated.

26.  By a decision of 26 July 2018, the Sabail District Court refused to hear the applicant’s complaint. It quoted the text of Article 449 of the CCrP without specifying how it was relevant to the case, saying that the measure complained of did not fall under the judicial supervision procedure according to Articles 442 and 449-451 of the CCrP.

27.  The applicant appealed against the decision, reiterating his previous arguments. On 27 August 2018 the Baku Court of Appeal gave a final decision in which it upheld the decision of the lower court, stating briefly that the complaints did not fall under the judicial supervision procedure.

28.  The seized laptop was recognised as physical evidence in the criminal proceedings by a decision of 6 December 2018 of the prosecuting authorities. In the same decision they also stated that the applicant’s two mobile telephones would be returned to him as there was no longer any need to retain them, but that pursuant to a certificate (arayış) annexed to a bill of indictment dated 15 December 2018 the laptop was being retained by the Baku City Prosecutor’s Office.

29.  The applicant claimed that the items were only returned to him five years later and in an unusable condition. The applicant claimed that the unusable condition of the items had been also noted in the record of the return of seized items (götürülmüş əşyaların qaytarılması haqqında protokol). The applicant also submitted that the record was held by the prosecuting authorities and that he had not been given a copy of it.

Criminal proceedings against the applicant and the trial

30.  On 10 July 2018 an expert forensic linguistic examination was ordered, presumably by the prosecuting authorities. Certain articles written by the applicant, including those mentioned above (see paragraphs 9, 12 and 13 above), were presented for examination and the expert was asked to determine whether those articles contained, inter alia, public calls against the State and its constitutional order and whether they cast a bad light over the government’s policies.

31.  On 31 October 2018 the appointed expert reported that the articles included public calls against the State which “openly incited the public to hatred towards the present government and the constitutional order, called on them to rise up against the authorities and engage in mass unrest, and encouraged them to disobey the lawful demands of government officials and commit other illegal actions”. In particular, the following statements – “Why does [I.A.] not see E.V.’s arbitrariness and rudeness, why does he not punish him? Or does [I.A.] say these things only for form’s sake?”, “... what happened to E.V. was bound to occur sooner or later. If the authorities do not draw conclusions from this, the events of Ismayilli and Quba may be repeated in Ganja” – were assessed as open calls against the State. According to the expert, those statements were calls to disrupt the country’s political stability and engage in mass unrest. The expert noted that the above statements could be used against the State in an “information war” given the geopolitical situation in the region. The report also stated that bias and provocation were obvious in the titles of the articles which were intended to defame the state authorities.

32.  On 12 December 2018 the applicant was formally charged with criminal offences under Articles 281.2 (open calls against the State, committed repeatedly or by a group of persons), 309.2 (exceeding the limits of authority, with the use of weapons or other devices, or when they result in serious consequences) and 313 (forgery by an official) of the Criminal Code. A bill of indictment was filed with the Baku Court of Serious Crimes.

33.  During the hearings in the Baku Court of Serious Crimes, the applicant requested an additional expert examination of the published articles, arguing that they contained no calls directed against the State. The court rejected the request. He further submitted that the information contained in the articles had previously been published by other media outlets and had not been retracted to date.

34.  On 18 March 2019 the Baku Court of Serious Crimes found the applicant guilty as charged on all counts and sentenced him to five years and six months’ imprisonment suspended on probation for two years and a two‑year ban on holding public office. The court relied to a significant extent on the above-mentioned forensic linguistic expert report, in which the expert had identified certain passages (see paragraph 9, 12 and 13 above) as containing elements of public calls against the State, and held that the articles contained such calls, which “openly incited the public to hatred towards the present government and the constitutional order, called on them to rise up against the authorities and engage in mass unrest, and encouraged them to disobey the lawful demands of government representatives and commit other illegal actions”. The court further held that by publishing the articles with the aim of creating negative public opinion among citizens about the Ganja events, disrupting the stability of the country’s social and political life, undermining trust in state‑organised mass events, and casting doubt on what the law‑enforcement agencies were doing in the fight against crime, the applicant had exceeded his official powers and committed forgery in his official role for personal purposes, causing significant harm and serious consequences to the legally protected interests of society and the State.

35.  The trial court also referred to the statements of two individuals from Baku, an old woman and her adult daughter, who complained to the prosecuting authorities that after reading those allegedly provocative articles published by the applicant, they had felt anxious, frightened, or distressed, and that they wanted the author to be punished. Those witnesses, who used similar wording to each other, had stated, inter alia, that, after reading those articles they were “afraid that unrest would break out in society” and that the author had blamed the government for the events occurred in Ganja and “attributed the incident [the assassination attempt in Ganja] to the people’s discontent”, which they considered to be agitation against the State. However, they did not specify which statements or remarks in the articles they considered to be provocative.

36.  The court also briefly referred to the unrest in Ganja on 10 July 2018, during which two police officers were killed (see paragraph 7 above) and dozens of individuals were arrested. The court, however, did not clarify why it referred to that incident in the present case, and what its relevance was to the subject matter of the case.

37.  The court further noted that the allegations in the article that there was a hostile relationship between E.V. and R.M. had been publicly refuted by R.M. himself as mere rumours in various media outlets as early as 2013, including the outlet cited by the applicant in his article, and there had been an official statement explaining the reasons for R.M.’s resignation. However, despite the previous warnings from the prosecuting authorities, the applicant had again disseminated unverified news in the mass media, which was prohibited by Article 10 of the Law on the Mass Media.

38.  The court also noted that even though the applicant claimed that he had been quoting other media outlets in the articles, he had changed the original title of the second article from “The authorities are trying to downplay the assassination attempt on the head of Ganja as an ordinary criminal incident” to “The Ganja events follow E.V.’s rudeness”, and had misrepresented the situation from personal motives.

39.  As regards the seized laptop, the court decided it should be returned after the judgment became final.

40.  The applicant appealed against the judgment, claiming that the criminal proceedings against him had been fabricated, and that they constituted an interference with his private life and with his professional life as a journalist. In particular, he argued that both articles contained, inter alia, information which had been published earlier by other media outlets which concerned matters of public interest and, in certain parts, his value judgments. He maintained that the trial court had misapplied the provisions of the Criminal Code to the facts of his case, because neither of his articles contained any calls against the State, nor had he “exceeded his official authority” as a journalist or committed forgery as an official. He further argued that the information in the articles he had quoted from had not been refuted, which meant that he could not be held liable. He further claimed that he had been convicted because of his activities as a journalist, with the aim of compelling him to self-censor and so as to hinder his activities. He also argued that the previous warnings of the prosecuting authorities (see paragraphs 6 and 15 above) had been wrongfully used as aggravating elements in the current proceedings.

41.  On 4 June 2019 the Baku Court of Appeal upheld the judgment of the lower court and endorsed its reasoning, without expressly addressing the applicant’s arguments.

42.  The applicant lodged a cassation appeal against the decision of the appellate court, reiterating his previous arguments.

43.  By a final judgment of 25 February 2020 the Supreme Court partially upheld the lower courts’ judgments convicting the applicant. It upheld the convictions on the charges under Articles 281.2 and 313 of the Criminal Code, but reclassified the offence from Article 309.2 to Article 309.1 of the Criminal Code (exceeding the limits of authority causing significant harm to the rights and lawful interests of natural or legal persons, or to the legally protected interests of society or the State) and reduced the sentence to five years and three months’ imprisonment suspended on probation for two years, together with the same additional sanction of two years’ ban on holding public office.

RELEVANT LEGAL FRAMEWORK
THE 2000 CRIMINAL CODE

44.  At the material time, Article 281 of the Criminal Code provided as follows:

Article 281. Open calls against the State

“281.1. Making open calls for the violent seizure or violent retention of power, or for the violent alteration of the constitutional order of the Republic of Azerbaijan, or for the violation of its territorial integrity, or distributing materials with similar content – is punishable by imprisonment for up to five years.

281.2. The same actions, when committed repeatedly or by a group of persons acting together – are punishable by imprisonment for a term of five to eight years.”

45.  At the material time, Article 309 of the Code provided:

Article 309. Exceeding the limits of authority

“309.1. When an official clearly exceeds the limits of their official authority and performs actions which cause significant harm to the rights and lawful interests of natural or legal persons, or to the legally protected interests of society or the state –

they will be punished with a fine from two thousand to four thousand manats, or with correctional labour for up to two years, or with deprivation of the right to hold certain positions or engage in certain activities for up to three years, or with imprisonment for up to three years.

309.2. The actions specified in Article 309.1, when committed with the use of force or threat of force, or with the use of weapons or other devices, or when they result in serious consequences –

will be punished with deprivation of the right to hold certain positions or engage in certain activities for up to three years, and with imprisonment for a term of three to eight years.”

46.  At the material time, Article 313 of the Code provided:

Article 313. Forgery by an official

“Forgery by an official, meaning the deliberate inclusion of false information by an official in official documents or information resources, or making alterations in documents or information resources so as to distort their original content, when such actions are committed for personal gain or from other personal motives –

is punishable by a fine from one thousand five hundred to three thousand manats, or by correctional labour for a term of one to two years, or by deprivation of the right to hold certain positions or engage in certain activities for up to two years, or by imprisonment for up to two years.”

The 2000 CODE OF CRIMINAL PROCEDURE

47.  The relevant provision of the CCrP concerning the powers of the investigator reads:

Article 85. Investigator

“85.4. In the cases and manner provided for in this Code, the investigator shall exercise the following powers:

...

85.4.2. to detain the suspect; to interrogate him or her, ... to order an expert examination; ... to carry out inspections, searches, seizures, examinations (including personal examination), and other investigative actions;

...”

48.  The relevant provisions of the CCrP concerning the material evidence and their retention read:

Article 128. Material Evidence

“128.1. Any item that, by its nature and characteristics, origin, place and time of discovery, or by bearing traces of the event, helps to determine circumstances significant for criminal prosecution may be considered physical evidence.

128.2. An item will be recognised as physical evidence by a decision of the body conducting the criminal proceedings.

...”

Article 129. Retention of material evidence and other items

“129.1. Material evidence shall be packaged as far as possible, sealed, and kept in the criminal case file. ...

...

129.4. Material evidence and other items seized in the case shall be kept by the authority conducting the criminal process until the lawful judgment of the court enters into force or until a decision is made to terminate the criminal prosecution. In cases provided for by this Code, a decision regarding material evidence may be made before the completion of the criminal prosecution.

...”

49.  The relevant provisions of the CCrP concerning the right to carry out investigative measures without consent provided as follows at the time of the events:

Article 177.  Right to carry out investigative measures without consent

“177.1.  The authority conducting criminal proceedings may carry out investigative measures without the consent of the party being investigated in order to ensure the normal course of the investigation ...

177.2.  If the conduct of an investigative measure is not authorised by the person concerned and authorisation by a court is required to carry it out, the prosecutor supervising the preliminary investigation, after a request with reasons from the investigator, must make an application to the court.

177.3.  The conduct of the investigative measures set out below without consent requires, as a general rule, authorisation by a court:

177.3.1.  conduct of inspection, search, seizure and other investigative measures in a residential place, office or industrial buildings;

...

177.3.5.  interception of conversations held by telephone and other means and of information sent via telecommunications and other technical means;

...

177.4.  inspection and other investigative measures in a residential place, service or industrial buildings and the investigative measures provided for by Articles 177.3.6 and 177.3.7 of this Code may be conducted only after authorisation by a court. The investigator may take his own decision and without obtaining a corresponding court order may carry out the following investigative actions without consent:

177.4.1.  inspection, search and seizure in a residential place, office or industrial buildings – when the grounds and circumstances provided for in Article 243.3 of this Code are present;

...

177.5.  ... The decision of the investigator shall give reasons why it is necessary and urgent to conduct an investigative measure without a court decision ...

177.6. When the investigative actions specified in Article 177.3.1 of this Code are carried out by the investigator at the invitation or with the permission of the person who resides at, works in, or owns the residential place, office, or industrial buildings in question, court authorisation is not required.”

50.  The relevant provisions of the CCrP concerning search and seizure provided as follows:

Article 243.  Grounds for conducting a search or seizure

“243.1.  As a rule, the search or seizure shall be carried out after authorisation by a court. The court shall deliver a decision on conducting a search or seizure following a request from the investigator giving reasons and the submissions of the prosecutor in charge of the investigation. The search or seizure must be carried out in compliance with the requirements in Articles 177.2.-177.6. of this Code.

243.2.  The decision on the search or seizure should specify the following:

243.2.1.  The date, time and place of the delivery of the decision;

243.2.2.  The name, surname, patronymic and position of the person delivering the decision;

243.2.3.  The justification of the objective facts and motives constituting grounds for the conduct of a search or seizure;

243.2.4.  The name, surname and patronymic of the person in respect of whom the search or seizure is to be conducted;

243.2.5.  The exact place (residential, service or industrial buildings, address or location) where the search or seizure will be conducted;

243.2.6.  If a decision authorises seizure, it shall also specify the items and documents to be seized.

243.3.  The investigator may in urgent circumstances conduct a search or seizure without a court decision only if there is precise information giving rise to a likelihood of the following:

243.3.1.  The concealment in a residential place of an item or document indicative of the commission of a criminal offence against a person or State authority or of preparation to commit such an offence;

...

243.4.  In the circumstances provided for by Article 243.3 the investigator must deliver a decision on the search or seizure and must give reasons. The investigator’s decision should be in compliance with the requirement of Article 243.2 of this Code taking into account the grounds for finding the search or seizure is sufficiently necessary and urgent for it to be conducted without authorisation by a court.”

51.  The relevant provisions of the CCrP concerning the investigative actions and operational measures carried out without consent authorised by a court decision, and the judicial supervision procedure, as in force at the relevant time, provided as follows:

Article 443. Investigative actions carried out without consent authorised by a court decision

“443.1. As a general rule, the investigative actions specified in Article 177.3 of this Code are carried out without consent on the basis of an authorisation by means of a court decision.

443.2. When the investigative actions specified in Articles 177.3.1–177.3.5 and 177.3.8 of this Code are carried out without consent on the basis of a reasoned decision of the investigator without a court decision, the investigator must, after completing the respective investigative action, fulfil the following requirements:

443.2.1. within 24 hours, inform the court exercising judicial supervision and the prosecutor exercising procedural supervision over the preliminary investigation about the investigative action that was carried out;

443.2.2. within 48 hours, submit to the court exercising judicial supervision and to the prosecutor exercising procedural supervision over the preliminary investigation the materials of the investigative action for the purpose of their confirming the legality of the action carried out.

...”

Article 445. Operational‑search measures carried out on the basis of a court decision

445.1. The following operational‑search measures shall be carried out on the basis of a court decision:

...

445.1.2. inspection of postal, telegraph, and other communications;

445.1.3. extraction of information from technical communication channels and other technical devices;

...

445.2. In the cases provided for in paragraph 4 of Article 10 of the Law of the Republic of Azerbaijan “On Operational‑Search Activity”, the operational‑search measures listed in Article 445.1 of this Code may be carried out without a court authorisation, on the basis of a decision giving reasons of an authorised official of the body conducting operational‑search activity. In such cases, after the relevant measure has been carried out, the authorised official of the body conducting operational‑search activity must submit the decision to conduct the operational‑search measure with the reasons for it to the court exercising judicial supervision and to the prosecutor supervising the preliminary investigation within 48 hours.”

Article 449. Filing a complaint with the court against procedural actions or decisions of the body conducting the criminal process

“...

449.2.  The following persons have the right to file a complaint against the procedural actions or decisions of the body conducting the criminal process:

449.2.1.  the accused person or suspect and his or her defence counsel;

449.2.2.  the victim and his or her legal representative;

449.2.3.  other persons whose rights and freedoms have been violated as a result of the procedural decision or act.

449.3.  The persons referred to in Article 449.2 of this Code shall have the right to complain to a court against procedural acts or decisions of an authority conducting criminal proceedings in connection with the following matters:

...

449.3.5.  a refusal to commence criminal proceedings or the suspension or termination of criminal proceedings;

449.3.6.  the conduct of an investigative action without consent, the application of a procedural coercive measure, or the carrying out of an operational‑search measure without a court decision;

...”

52.  In 2024, the following paragraphs were inserted in the text of Article 443 of the CCrP:

“...

443.3. After receiving the material specified in Article 443.2.2 of this Code, the court exercising judicial supervision shall, within 48 hours, check the lawfulness of the investigative action carried out without the authorisation of a court, in accordance with the procedure set out in Article 447 of this Code.

443.4. On the basis of that check, the judge must issue a decision giving reasons either recognising the investigative action as lawful or, if it has been found to have been unlawful, cancelling the decision to carry out the investigative action without the authorisation of a court.

443.5. A copy of the judge’s decision as regards the lawfulness of the investigative action shall be sent immediately after it is given to the investigator who took the decision to conduct the investigative action, to the prosecutor exercising procedural supervision over the preliminary investigation, and to the person whose rights were affected by that decision, as well as to that person’s defence counsel or legal representative.

443.6. If the decision to conduct the investigative action is found to have been unlawful, the prosecutor exercising procedural supervision over the preliminary investigation, or a higher-ranking prosecutor, shall take immediate measures pursuant to the judge’s decision to end the violations of the person’s rights and freedoms and to restore the rights and freedoms which were breached.”

The 1999 law on operational-search activities

53.  The relevant provision on the operational-search measures which can be carried out without a court order reads as follow:

Article 10. Operational-search measures

“IV. Where there are grounds in the legislation of the Republic of Azerbaijan, those carrying out operational‑search activity may, without authorisation by a judge:

1) ... inspect postal, telegraph, and other communications, extract information from technical communication channels and other technical devices, ... for the purpose of preventing serious crimes against person or particularly serious crimes against the State;

... ”

THE 1999 LAW ON THE MASS MEDIA

54.  The relevant provision in force at the material time provided as follows (this Law was repealed in 2021):

Article 10. Prohibition of abusing the freedom of the mass media

“It is not permitted to use the mass media for the purpose of disseminating secrets protected by legislation of the Republic of Azerbaijan, or other information whose distribution is prohibited; to call for the violent overthrow of the present constitutional order, to undermine the territorial integrity of the state, to promote war, violence, or cruelty, or to incite national, racial, or social hatred or intolerance; to publish rumours, false or biased writing that insults the honour and dignity of citizens under the guise of a credible source; to publish pornographic material; to commit slander; or to engage in any other unlawful acts.”

The 1999 decision of parliament on the procedure for applying certain provisions of the Criminal Code of the Republic of Azerbaijan

“...

2. In Article 63 (currently Article 281 of the Criminal Code) of the Criminal Code of the Republic of Azerbaijan, the term “calls” refers to active actions aimed at influencing people’s will and encouraging them to commit the acts specified in this article. Mass character is a mandatory element of a call. When assessing whether a call is of a mass character, factors such as the place, method, specific circumstances, and other conditions of the call must be taken into account. In any case, for a call to be made to a mass audience, it must be received by two or more persons. Communication through television, radio, loudspeakers, distributing leaflets, or holding rallies are examples of mass calls.

...”
