case_name: CASE OF MÜYESSER UĞUR v. TÜRKİYE
full_case_text_no_verdict:
SECOND SECTION

CASE OF MÜYESSER UĞUR v. TÜRKİYE

(Application no. 45738/22)



JUDGMENTSTRASBOURG

6 October 2026



This judgment will become final in the circumstances set out in Article 44 § 2 of the Convention. It may be subject to editorial revision.

In the case of Müyesser Uğur v. Türkiye,

The European Court of Human Rights (Second Section), sitting as a Chamber composed of:

Arnfinn Bårdsen, President,
Saadet Yüksel,
Jovan Ilievski,
Oddný Mjöll Arnardóttir,
Gediminas Sagatys,
Juha Lavapuro,
Hugh Mercer, judges,
and Andrea Tamietti, Section Registrar,

Having regard to:

the application (no. 45738/22) against the Republic of Türkiye lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a Turkish national, Ms Müyesser Uğur (“the applicant”), on 12 September 2022;

the decision to give notice to the Turkish Government (“the Government”) of the complaints concerning the right to freedom of expression and the right to liberty and security, and to declare inadmissible the remainder of the application;

the parties’ observations;

Having deliberated in private on 1 September 2026,

Delivers the following judgment, which was adopted on that date:

INTRODUCTION

1.  The application concerns the pre-trial detention of the applicant, an investigative journalist, who was charged with disclosing confidential information relating to the security and political interests of the State on account of articles published on a news website. The case raises issues under Articles 5 and 10 of the Convention.

THE FACTS

2.  The applicant was born in 1963 and lives in Ankara. She was represented by Mr E. Tokatlı, a lawyer practising in Ankara.

3.  The Government were represented by their Agent at the time, Mr Hacı Ali Açıkgül, former Head of the Department of Human Rights of the Ministry of Justice of the Republic of Türkiye.

4.  The facts of the case may be summarised as follows.

I.        The applicant’s professional career and the articles leading to her pre-trial detention

5.  The applicant is a journalist who has written columns in numerous newspapers and websites on various political issues in Türkiye such as military-political relations, domestic politics and national security.

6.  At the time of the events giving rise to the present application, the applicant was publishing articles on a news website called odatv.com concerning a military cooperation agreement signed between the Turkish Government and the Libyan Government of National Accord, and the subsequent deployment of troops of the Turkish Armed Forces to Libya.[1]

7.  On 19 December 2019 the applicant published an article entitled “Libya’ya ne tür ‘asker’ gönderilecek?” (“What kind of ‘soldiers’ will be sent to Libya?”), the relevant parts of which read as follows:

“... At the beginning of the article, we mentioned that Erdoğan cited the example of a ‘Russian security company’ regarding sending troops to Libya.

[A.T.], a retired major general [who is] Erdoğan’s chief advisor ... stated ... that countries like the United States of America, Russia, and the United Kingdom had had [at various times] private military companies and had used them in places where their armed forces had not been present. He emphasised that Türkiye definitely needed such a company.

Furthermore, [A.T.] argued that it would be better to send troops to Libya through private military companies, saying ‘The Turkish Armed Forces (TSK) exist for the security of our country. If we allocate part of it there, we will be reducing its presence in other areas. If we do it [through private military companies] it won’t be a burden on the TSK. The country [would receive] foreign currency income as though [from] an export product. It [would be] more beneficial to carry out this task through such private companies rather than sending our own TSK there.’

Now let’s ask:

If it happens, what kind of ‘soldiers’ will be sent to Libya...? Do both Erdoğan and Bahçeli understand the same thing by ‘sending soldiers’...? And does Bahçeli also support the idea of ‘military companies’?”

8.  On 24 December 2019 the applicant published another article, entitled “Kim bu Hafter’le görüşen Türk komutanlar” (“Who are these Turkish commanders who met with Haftar?”). The relevant parts of that article read as follows:

“... Let’s move on to another allegation.

Two days ago, Greek Foreign Minister [N.D.] was in Libya. He met with General Haftar. He said that the agreements made between Türkiye and the Government of National Accord had been contrary to international law.

What we want to draw attention to is a statement in the Greek newspaper To Vima, which reported these visits of [N.D.].

The newspaper reported that [N.D.], who stayed in Benghazi for a short time and [also] travelled to Cairo, had said that ‘Haftar was very glad that he had met with two Turkish commanders of the Libyan National Army’.

Is this true? If it is true, who are these two ‘Turkish commanders’? Are they retired, on active duty or NATO/US-backed ‘FETÖ’ fugitives?”

9.  On 20 January 2020 the applicant published another article, entitled “Libya’ya hangi komutan gitti?.. Yerine kim geldi?” (“Which commander went to Libya? Who replaced him?”), the relevant parts of which read as follows:

“After Parliament’s resolution (tezkere) to send troops to Libya, Erdoğan made the following statements in a television programme of 5 January regarding the mission of Turkish troops and who would be in charge of the operations centre to be established there:

‘Our soldiers’ duty there is coordination in terms of organising training and education programmes among all our security institutions. They are currently carrying out this coordination. There will be an operations centre there and a lieutenant general of ours will be present in this operations centre. They will manage this process there. The [soldiers] are already gradually [being sent there]. ... Currently, as a combat force, we will have different teams there. They will not be drawn from among our soldiers. These combat forces will work there with different teams. But the coordination will be handled by our senior soldiers ... Including our lieutenant general, and along with our lieutenant general, we will have well-trained teams who [will] make up the chain of command there. We will manage this process with them.’

We talk about Libya every day but, interestingly, no one has wondered, asked or written about who the commander of the Turkish force in Libya is or will be since that [statement by Erdoğan]. [The only follow up has been that] some websites reported that Brigadier General [H.S.], the Commander of the Şırnak Infantry Division, had been appointed to Libya, even though Erdoğan said ‘We will have a lieutenant general there’.

CHARACTERISTICS OF THAT COMMANDER

According to the information we have obtained, Lieutenant General [M.G.], the Deputy Chief of the General Staff, has been sent to Libya.

Let us remind you who Lieutenant General [M.G.] is.

During [the] 15 July [coup attempt] he was the commander of the 4th Army Corps and the Ankara Garrison. During the coup attempt he was one of the officers that were taken to Akıncı after being falsely imprisoned [by soldiers participating in the coup d’état] at the General Staff Headquarters. Let us summarise the experiences of (M.G.) [after his release: he] went to the Etimesgut Armoured Units School and Army Aviation Command on the order of [H.A.], the then Chief of the General Staff, and conveyed [H.A.]’s orders ‘There will be no tank movement until further orders, and no aircraft will fly’, according to his own statement ...

...

After 15 July, [M.G.], who was [made] the commander of Combat Service Support Training at the Land Forces Training and Doctrine Command and commander of the Kocaeli Garrison, and then the Chief of Staff of the Land Forces Command, was appointed as the Deputy Chief of the General Staff in 2018, replacing [Ü.D.], who was appointed as the Land Forces Commander.

The remarkable and unique thing about this appointment was that, excluding the one-year period during the 1960 coup d’état, this was the first time since 1943 that the position of the Deputy Chief of the General Staff had been filled by an officer with the rank of lieutenant general [rather than by a full general].

In the 2019 [Supreme Military Council], it was expected that [M.G.], who had completed four years as lieutenant general, would be promoted to the rank of full general, but that expectation did not materialise, and his appointment was extended.

Lieutenant General [M.G.], who was born in Mardin, is fluent in Arabic as well as in English.

ACTING DEPUTY CHIEF OF THE GENERAL STAFF

After Lieutenant General [M.G.] was assigned to Libya, Lieutenant General [S.B.] was appointed as acting Deputy Chief of the General Staff.

[S.B.], who had been serving as the Chief of Staff and Garrison Commander of the 3rd Army in Erzincan during the 15 July [coup attempt] and had been appointed Chief of Personnel of the General Staff upon his promotion to lieutenant general in 2016, was expected to be promoted to full general in the 2019 Supreme Military Council, but he had remained as a lieutenant general.

Ten days ago, [S.B.] was appointed as the Deputy Chief of the General Staff and it was learned that he will also continue to serve as the Chief of Personnel.

It should be noted that the dispatch of [M.G.] to Libya and the appointment of [S.B.] as the Deputy Chief of the General Staff already give important clues about the 2020 Supreme Military Council decisions.”

10.  On 23 February 2020 the applicant published an article titled “Suriye Milli Ordusu” ne zaman, nasıl ve hangi sıfatla Libya’ya gitti” (“When, how and in what capacity did the Syrian National Army go to Libya”). The relevant parts of that article read as follows:

“During his speech at the opening of the Northern Aegean Motorway in Izmir yesterday, Erdoğan said verbatim: ‘We sat down with the legitimate Prime Minister and administration of Libya, and signed the agreements. ... We are there against the illegitimate Haftar, against the mercenary Haftar, with our heroic soldiers and teams from the Syrian National Army ...’

...

Whenever the issue of Libya comes up, Erdoğan has reacted to the Wagner company and Russia as follows: ‘The 5,000 who came from Sudan, the 2,000 who came from Russia under the name Wagner, by what right did they come, what are they doing there?’

Given this situation, how is it that Erdoğan openly declares that the ‘Syrian National Army’ is in Libya?

Now, couldn’t Russia first say ‘in what capacity did the Syrians come, what are they doing there?’

By the way, when and how did the ‘Syrian National Army Troops’ go to Libya?

...

Did [Parliament] know that the ‘Syrian National Army’ would also be sent to Libya when it passed the resolution (tezkere)? Let’s look at the resolution passed on 2 January:

...

What does it mention? Only the Turkish Armed Forces ...

...

Let’s immediately recall Erdoğan’s statement on a television programme three days after the resolution was accepted:

‘Our soldiers’ duty there is coordination in terms of organising training and education programmes among all our security institutions. They are currently carrying out this coordination. There will be an operations centre there and a lieutenant general of ours will be present in this operations centre. They will manage this process there. The [soldiers] are already gradually [being sent there]. ... Currently, as a combat force, we will have different teams there. They will not be drawn from among our soldiers. These combat forces will work there with different teams. But the coordination will be handled by our senior soldiers ... Including our lieutenant general, and along with our lieutenant general, we will have well-trained teams who [will] make up the chain of command there. We will manage this process with them.’

It is understood that the said ‘different teams’ that will be ‘a combat force’ are to be drawn from the ‘Syrian National Army’ and they are working under the ‘coordination’ of the Turkish Armed Forces...! What is the legal and political [basis for] this situation?”

11.  The applicant published two other articles, entitled “[H.A.] bizim kardeşimizdir” (“[H.A.] is our brother”) and “Ne yani devletin gazetesi de mi yalan yazdı” (“So did the State newspaper lie too?”), on the same website on 23 May 2018 and 25 November 2019 respectively. In those articles the applicant addressed issues such as the incriminating statements made by certain defendants regarding the Chief of the General Staff at public hearings held within the scope of criminal proceedings on the attempted coup d’état of 15 July 2016, and allegations raised in public by a member of the Turkish Parliament that a religious foundation had begun to take over key positions in two defence industry companies.

II.      The criminal investigation against the applicant and her pre-trial detention

A.   Inclusion of the applicant in the criminal investigation against E.B. and her arrest

12.  On 13 November 2019 the Ankara Chief Public Prosecutor’s Office received a tip-off that E.B., a sergeant at the Hadımköy Military Barracks, had been leaking confidential information concerning certain military operations.

13.  On 3 December 2019 the Ankara 4th Magistrate’s Court ordered the wiretapping of E.B.’s phone communications. Within the scope of that wiretapping measure, phone calls between the applicant and E.B. were intercepted. Those communications mainly concerned the ongoing military operations conducted by the Turkish Armed Forces in Libya and Syria.

14.  On 9 January 2020, following the interception of the phone conversations between E.B. and the applicant, the Ankara 7th Magistrate’s Court ordered the wiretapping of the applicant’s phone communications.

15.  According to the wiretapping records, during a phone call on 13 January 2020 the applicant asked E.B. who the high-level commander being sent to Libya to take charge of the operation there would be and E.B. told here that it would be M.G., the then Deputy Chief of the General Staff (Genelkurmay İkinci Başkanı).

16.  On 15 April 2020 the Ankara 7th Magistrate’s Court decided to restrict the suspects’ access to the investigation file.

17.  On 8 June 2020 both E.B. and the applicant were arrested, and the applicant’s home was searched by the police.

B.   The questioning of the applicant by the police and the public prosecutor

18.  On 11 June 2020, during the questioning of the applicant by the police officers and the public prosecutor, she was asked about the content of her phone communications with E.B. and about her articles, in particular the ones titled “Who are these Turkish commanders who met with Haftar?” and “Which commander went to Libya? Who replaced him?” (see paragraphs 8 and 9 above). The applicant was asked whether she had published those articles in the light of information she had allegedly obtained from E.B. The applicant did not deny her relationship with E.B. but stated that none of her articles had contained State secrets and that she had never obtained or published State secrets. She further stated that E.B. had only been in touch with her by phone and that he had not sent any documents to her although she had asked him to share documents concerning certain points which he had mentioned.

19.  On the same date the Ankara Provincial Directorate of Security submitted a report to the public prosecutor. In that report it was stated that in her articles titled “What kind of ‘soldiers’ will be sent to Libya?”, “Who are these Turkish commanders who met with Haftar?”, “Which commander went to Libya? Who replaced him?”, “When, how and in what capacity did the Syrian National Army go to Libya?”, “[H.A.] is our brother” and “So did the State newspaper lie too?” (see paragraphs 7-11 above), the applicant had mentioned confidential information she had obtained from E.B.

20.  On the same date the public prosecutor transferred the applicant to the Ankara 3rd Magistrate’s Court and requested that she be placed in pre-trial detention. In his request, the public prosecutor argued, on the basis of the wiretapping records, that the applicant’s articles, such as “Which commander went to Libya? Who replaced him?” and “When, how and in what capacity did the Syrian National Army go to Libya?” (see paragraphs 9 and 10 above), had been written based on secret information leaked by E.B. and that the applicant had also requested numerous documents from E.B. concerning military issues such as an amendment to regulations on martyr ceremonies, the transfer of certain military barracks within the scope of a government project and a report on ill-disciplined acts by certain Turkish soldiers on the Türkiye-Syria border. Then he concluded that the applicant should be placed in pre-trial detention on charges of disclosing information relating to the security and political interests of the State under Article 329 § 1 of the Criminal Code (see paragraph 44 below).

C.   The applicant’s questioning at the magistrate’s court and the subsequent decision ordering her initial pre-trial detention

21.  At the Ankara 3rd Magistrate’s Court, the applicant repeated her denial of all the accusations, arguing that there was no link between the articles being investigated and her communications with E.B. She further stated that all her articles had been based on publicly available information and that she was a journalist who followed developments within the Turkish military. Her lawyers argued that for her to be convicted of the relevant offence there would have had to have been an imminent and concrete risk to the security and interests of the State, which they denied existed, and submitted that the applicant’s articles had been based on open sources. As for the article entitled “Which commander went to Libya? Who replaced him?” (see paragraph 9 above), they argued, in particular, that the President of the Republic had already declared at the material time that a lieutenant general had been assigned for the military operation in Libya, and that M.G. had been one of only a few lieutenant generals in the Turkish Army at the material time. As for the article titled “Who are these Turkish commanders who met with Haftar?” (see paragraph 8 above), they claimed that it had been stated in the article that certain fugitive Fetullahist ex-military officers had met with Khalifa Belqasım Haftar, the commander of the Tobruk-based Libyan National Army. They further pointed out that access to the articles in question had not been blocked despite the fact that they had been published several months earlier.

22.  On 11 June 2020, following the questioning of the applicant and E.B., the Ankara 3rd Magistrate’s Court decided to place them in pre-trial detention on charges of disclosing information relating to the security and political interests of the State. The relevant part of the detention order reads as follows:

“... [A strong suspicion has been] established that suspects E.B. and [the applicant] committed the offence of disclosing confidential information relating to the security and political interests of the state; there is a strong suspicion that the suspects have committed the offence based on the conversations in the wiretapping records ([the accuracy of] which was accepted by the suspects), the content of [the applicant]’s articles, the reports on the seized digital materials and the entirety of the case file; if the suspects are released they could affect the evidence since the investigation is ongoing and the evidence has not been fully collected; if the [criminality of the] suspects’ acts is ... established there would be a risk of their absconding given the potential sentence they would be liable to serve; [in the light of the above] judicial control measures alone would not be sufficient, and since it has been concluded that detention is proportionate, it has been decided that the suspects should be placed separately in pre-trial detention in accordance with Articles 100 et seq. of the [Code of Criminal Procedure] ...”

23.  On 16 June 2020 the applicant lodged an appeal against the pre-trial detention order. In a decision of 23 June 2020 the Ankara 4th Magistrate’s Court dismissed the appeal, on the basis of the case file, holding that the detention decision was in line with domestic law.

24.  The magistrates’ courts extended the applicant’s pre-trial detention on several occasions until the bill of indictment was issued by the public prosecutor. In doing so, they relied in particular on the nature of the offence, the state of the evidence, the fact that the investigation had not yet been concluded, the risk of tampering with evidence, the existence of a strong suspicion that the applicant had committed the offence, the proportionality of the detention measure, and the insufficiency of judicial control.

III.    Bill of indictment and the ensuing criminal proceedings

25.  During the criminal investigation the public prosecutor requested information from the Ministry of National Defence concerning the alleged confidential nature of the information collected by the applicant.

26.  In its response, the Ministry of National Defence stated that the information given by E.B. to the applicant, namely that “the Commander of the Libya Task Force was Lieutenant General [M.G.] and he had already gone to Libya” was accurate. It was also noted that the confidentiality levels of the relevant documents containing that information were “Confidential (1), Confidential (2).”

27.  On 23 September 2020 the Ankara Chief Public Prosecutor’s Office issued a bill of indictment. The public prosecutor argued that most of the information which E.B. had shared with the applicant had been classified as confidential. According to the public prosecutor, the applicant had been constantly in contact with E.B. and had frequently sought classified information from him concerning the military operations in Syria and Libya. He argued that the applicant had written many articles containing information she had obtained from E.B. as a result of those conversations. In the bill of indictment the public prosecutor referred in particular to six articles, entitled “What kind of ‘soldiers’ will be sent to Libya?”, “Who are these Turkish commanders who met with Haftar?”, “Which commander went to Libya? Who replaced him?”, “When, how and in what capacity did the Syrian national army go to Libya?”, “[H.A.] is our brother” and “So did the State newspaper lie too?” (see paragraphs 7-11 above).

28.  On 29 September 2020 the Ankara 26th Assize Court accepted the bill of indictment and the criminal proceedings commenced.

29.  At the end of a hearing held on 9 November 2020 the applicant was released subject to measures of judicial control.

30.  On 11 December 2020 the public prosecutor filed another bill of indictment, charging the applicant with obtaining information on State security under Article 327 § 1 of the Criminal Code (see paragraph 44 below), based on the allegation that she had obtained the above-mentioned confidential information. On 14 December 2020 that bill of indictment was accepted and the two criminal proceedings were joined.

31.  On 8 March 2021 the Ankara 26th Assize Court sentenced the applicant to one year and ten days’ imprisonment for the offence of obtaining prohibited information under Article 334 § 1 of the Criminal Code, and to two years and six months’ imprisonment for the offence of disclosing prohibited information under Article 336 § 1 of the Criminal Code (see paragraph 44 below). It decided to only suspend the sentence handed down to her under Article 334 § 1 of the Criminal Code on the grounds that the sentence handed down in respect of the other offence exceeded the statutory threshold for suspension, namely two years.

32.  The trial court ordered the applicant’s immediate detention upon conviction.

33.   In its reasoning the trial court found that only the article entitled “Which commander went to Libya? Who replaced him?” contained information deemed significant for State interests, whereas the remaining articles did not disclose any information amounting to a criminal offence. It further noted that although the applicant had been charged with obtaining and disclosing information relating to the security and political interests of the State under Articles 327 and 329 of the Criminal Code, the information obtained and disclosed by the applicant was not a State secret, but rather information prohibited from disclosure falling within the scope of Articles 334 and 336 of the Criminal Code. As a result, the trial court acquitted the applicant of the offences under Articles 327 and 329 of the Criminal Code.

34.  The applicant appealed against her conviction.

35.  On 3 November 2022 the 4th Chamber of the Ankara Court of Appeals upheld the above-mentioned convictions with final effect. It also upheld the acquittals on the charges brought under Articles 327 and 329 of the Criminal Code, subject to appeal before the Court of Cassation.

36.  At the date of the latest information available to the Court (2 April 2024), the criminal proceedings were still pending before the domestic courts, the applicant having lodged an appeal with the Court of Cassation.

IV.   The applicant’s individual application to the Constitutional Court

37.  On 3 July 2020, following the decision of the Ankara 4th Magistrate’s Court dated 23 June 2020 (see paragraph 23 above), the applicant lodged an individual application with the Constitutional Court.

38.  On 7 April 2022 the Constitutional Court, sitting in a plenary formation composed of fifteen judges, held by a majority that the applicant’s placement in pre-trial detention had not breached her right to liberty and security under Article 19 of the Constitution or her right to freedom of expression under Article 26 of the Constitution.

39.  In examining the applicant’s complaints under Article 19 of the Constitution, the Constitutional Court acknowledged that the applicant had been placed in pre-trial detention on the basis of the charge of disclosing confidential information under Article 329 of the Criminal Code and not of obtaining confidential information under Article 327 of the Criminal Code (see paragraph 44 below), but it decided nonetheless to examine the detention order in the light of both offences. It noted in that respect that the applicant had later been charged with both offences (see paragraph 30 above), and that those offences were intertwined, which could in certain cases result in different assessments by the domestic courts as to the classification of similar acts.

40.  The Constitutional Court’s assessment, in so far as it concerned the existence of a reasonable suspicion in respect of the offence of disclosing confidential information, reads as follows:

“64. In terms of the offence of disclosing confidential information, it was alleged that the applicant compiled confidential information obtained from a certain E.B. and published it on the ODA TV website. It was alleged by the investigating authorities that E.B., as a soldier, conveyed to the applicant confidential information which he had obtained in various ways and which had been of a confidential nature in terms of the security [and] domestic or foreign political interests of the State. It was also alleged that the applicant, as a journalist, disclosed this information to the public under the name of journalistic activity [there]by exceeding the legal limits defined for freedom of the press. The indictment included six articles of the applicant in this context. However, only two of those articles were associated with the information stated to be confidential.

65. Those two articles are ‘When, how and in what capacity did the Syrian National Army go to Libya?’ (dated 23 February 2020) and ‘Which commander went to Libya? Who replaced him?’ (dated 20 January 2020). In the article dated 23 February 2020, confidential information stating that ‘the Siirt Commando Brigade was preparing for the mission to Libya’ was not included. On the other hand, the article dated 20 January 2020 contains confidential information about the commander to be sent to Libya. Therefore, it is understood that the only evidence to support the allegation that [the applicant] disclosed confidential information is the article dated 20 January 2020.

66. The information disclosed in that article concerns the identity of the commander to be sent to Libya. In the context of the special circumstances of the ... case, it cannot be said that the disclosure of information about the commander to be sent to Libya at a time of live armed conflicts was not capable of causing a potential danger to national security and the right to life of the commander whose name was disclosed. Therefore, it has been concluded that [the magistrate’s court] sufficiently demonstrated that the information in question [could have] cause[d] serious damage and danger to national security or international relations, as stated in the judgment of the Court of Cassation. Therefore, it cannot be said that the assessments made by the investigation authorities and the judicial bodies deciding on the [pre-trial] detention that there [we]re strong indications of a criminal offence in terms of the offence of disclosing information relating to the security and political interests of the State were ill-founded.”

41.  In terms of whether there had been a reasonable suspicion as to the offence of obtaining confidential information, the Constitutional Court listed several pieces of information which the applicant had obtained from E.B. Noting that most of that information was sensitive and relevant to the security and interests of the State, the Constitutional Court found that the domestic courts’ assessment as to the existance of a reasonable suspicion that the applicant might have committed the offence under Article 327 of the Criminal Code could not be regarded unreasonable.

42.  The Constitutional Court also found that there had been no violation of the applicant’s right to freedom of expression on the grounds that there was no reason for it to depart from its assessment under the right to liberty and security.

43.  Four judges disagreed with the majority’s conclusion regarding both of the applicant’s complaints. In their dissenting opinions, written separately by each of them, they opined that the assessment of strong suspicion should have been made only in respect of the offence under Article 329 of the Criminal Code since the applicant had not been detained for the offence under Article 327 of the same code. As regards the existence of a strong suspicion in respect of the article entitled “Which commander went to Libya? Who replaced him?” (see paragraph 9 above), they noted firstly that the rank of the commander assigned to Libya had already been disclosed by the Government and had therefore become public to a certain extent before the publication of the applicant’s article. In their opinion it was not clear that a lawful administrative decision had been made to prohibit the disclosure of relevant information. They further considered that the investigative authorities had failed to demonstrate how the disclosure in question would harm national security and international affairs. They also noted that in any event the grounds for detention referred to by the magistrate’s court had been formulaic and abstract. In their view, the applicant’s placement in pre-trial detention had not been necessary or proportionate given that she had been placed in detention five months after the publication of her article and three months after the wiretapping measure had been ordered, and that during her pre-trial detention no fresh evidence had been collected.

RELEVANT LEGAL FRAMEWORK AND PRACTICE

Domestic Law

44.  The relevant provisions of the Criminal Code, in force at the relevant time, are as follows:



Article 327

“(1) Anyone who procures information that, due to its nature, must remain confidential for reasons relating to the security of the State or its domestic or foreign political interests shall be sentenced to a penalty of imprisonment for a term of three to eight years.”

Article 329

“(1) Anyone who discloses information which, due to its nature, must remain confidential for reasons relating to the security of the State or its domestic or foreign political interests shall be sentenced to a penalty of imprisonment for a term of five to ten years.”

Article 334

“Anyone who procures information which, due to its nature, must remain confidential and the disclosure of which has been prohibited by competent authorities in accordance with the law and regulatory acts shall be sentenced to a penalty of imprisonment for a term of one to three years.”

Article 336

“Anyone who discloses information which, due to its nature, must remain confidential and the disclosure of which has been prohibited by competent authorities in accordance with the law and regulatory acts shall be sentenced to a penalty of imprisonment for a term of three to five years.”

II.      International Materials

45.  Recommendation No. R (2000) 7 of the Council of Europe’s Committee of Ministers to member States on the rights of journalists not to disclose their sources of information states that the following measures should not be applied if their purpose was to circumvent the right of journalists not to disclose information identifying a source:

“i. interception orders or actions concerning communication or correspondence of journalists or their employers,

ii. surveillance orders or actions concerning journalists, their contacts or their employers;

iii. search or seizure orders or actions concerning the private or business premises, belongings or correspondence of journalists or their employers[,] or personal data related to their professional work.”

46.  On 19 April 2007 the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe (PACE) adopted Resolution 1551 (2007) on fair trial issues in criminal cases concerning espionage or divulging State secrets. The paragraphs of relevance to the present case read as follows:

“1. The Parliamentary Assembly finds that the State’s legitimate interest in protecting official secrets must not become a pretext to unduly restrict the freedom of expression and of information, international scientific co-operation and the work of lawyers and other defenders of human rights.

2. It recalls the importance of freedom of expression and of information in a democratic society, in which it must be possible to freely expose corruption, human rights violations, environmental destruction and other abuses of authority.

...

5. The Assembly notes that legislation on official secrecy in many Council of Europe member States is rather vague or otherwise overly broad in that it could be construed in such a way as to cover a wide range of legitimate activities of journalists, scientists, lawyers or other human rights defenders.

6. ... For its part, the European Court of Human Rights found ‘disproportionate’ an injunction against the publication in the United Kingdom of newspaper articles reporting on the contents of a book (Spycatcher) that allegedly contained secret information, as the book was readily available abroad.

...

9. It calls on the judicial authorities of all countries concerned and on the European Court of Human Rights to find an appropriate balance between the State interest in preserving official secrecy on the one hand, and freedom of expression and of the free flow of information on scientific matters, and society’s interest in exposing abuses of power on the other hand.

10. The Assembly notes that criminal trials for breaches of State secrecy are particularly sensitive and prone to abuse for political purposes. It therefore considers the following principles as vital for all those concerned in order to ensure fairness in such trials:

10.1. information that is already in the public domain cannot be considered as a State secret, and divulging such information cannot be punished as espionage, even if the person concerned collects, sums up, analyses or comments on such information. The same applies to participation in international scientific co-operation, and to the exposure of corruption, human rights violations, environmental destruction or other abuses of public authority (whistle-blowing);”

47.  On 26 September 2007 the Committee of Ministers of the Council of Europe adopted a Declaration on the Protection and Promotion of Investigative Journalism, the relevant parts of which read as follows:

“4. Acknowledging, in this context, the important work of investigative journalists who engage in accurate, in-depth and critical reporting on matters of special public concern, work which often requires long and difficult research, assembling and analysing information, uncovering unknown facts, verifying assumptions and obtaining corroborative evidence;

...

7. Considering that, because of its very nature, investigative journalism is of particular significance in times of crisis, a notion that includes, but is not limited to, wars, terrorist attacks and natural and man-made disasters, when there may be a temptation to limit the free flow of information for security or public safety reasons; ...

II. Calls on member states to protect and promote investigative journalism, having regard to Article 10 of the European Convention on Human Rights, the relevant case law of the European Court of Human Rights and other Council of Europe standards, and in this context:

...

iv. to ensure that deprivation of liberty, disproportionate pecuniary sanctions, prohibition to exercise the journalistic profession, seizure of professional material or search of premises are not misused to intimidate media professionals and, in particular, investigative journalists;

...”
target_question: whether the Court finds a violation by Türkiye of Article 10 (Freedom of expression) concerning Freedom of expression in this case

case_name: CASE OF KOSTOV v. HUNGARY
full_case_text_no_verdict:
SECOND SECTION

CASE OF KOSTOV v. HUNGARY

(Application no. 7869/25)





JUDGMENTSTRASBOURG

6 October 2026





This judgment will become final in the circumstances set out in Article 44 § 2 of the Convention. It may be subject to editorial revision.



In the case of Kostov v. Hungary,

The European Court of Human Rights (Second Section), sitting as a Chamber composed of:

Arnfinn Bårdsen, President,
Jovan Ilievski,
Péter Paczolay,
Oddný Mjöll Arnardóttir,
Stéphane Pisani,
Juha Lavapuro,
Hugh Mercer, judges,
and Andrea Tamietti, Section Registrar,

Having regard to:

the application (no. 7869/25) against Hungary lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a Slovak national, Mr Norbert Kostov (“the applicant”), on 28 February 2025;

the decision to give notice to the Hungarian Government (“the Government”) of the complaint concerning Article 5 § 3 of the Convention and to declare the remainder of the application inadmissible;

the decision of the Government of the Slovak Republic not to intervene in the case;

the parties’ observations;

Having deliberated in private on 8 September 2026,

Delivers the following judgment, which was adopted on that date:

INTRODUCTION

1.  The case concerns the applicant’s complaint under Article 5 § 3 of the Convention that his pre-trial detention was unreasonably long and lacked adequate justification.

THE FACTS

2.  The applicant was born in 1978. At the time of introduction of the application to the Court, he was detained in Hungary, at Budapest Correctional Facility (Fővárosi Büntetés-végrehajtási Intézet). He was represented by Mr L. Jován, a lawyer practising in Budapest.

3.  The Government were represented by their Agent, Mr Z. Tallódi of the Ministry of Justice.

4.  The facts of the case may be summarised as follows.

5.  A criminal investigation into a double homicide committed by Slovak nationals was begun after the discovery in Hungary on 9 July 2018 of human remains which had apparently been hidden there in February 2016.

6.  In February 2019 the offices of the Hungarian Attorney General and the Prosecutor General of the Slovak Republic set up a joint investigation team to coordinate a cross-border investigation into the deaths.

7.  A European Arrest Warrant was issued by the Buda Central District Court on 20 July 2020. The applicant was arrested on 24 July 2020 by the Slovak authorities and handed over to their Hungarian counterparts.

8.  On the same day the applicant was heard by the Hungarian police as a suspect in a homicide committed against multiple persons with premeditation and for gain (section 160 (1) and (2)(a)(b) and (f) of Act no. C of 2012 on the Criminal Code; hereinafter, “the Criminal Code”).

9.  On the application of the Budapest Chief Prosecution Office (Fővárosi Főügyészség), on 26 July 2020 the investigating judge of the Buda Central District Court (Budai Központi Kerületi Bíróság) ordered the applicant to be remanded in detention under section 271 (1) and (2) and section 276 (2)(a)(ab); (b)(bb) and (c)(cb) of Act no. XC of 2017 on the Code of Criminal Procedure (hereinafter, “the Code of Criminal Procedure” – see paragraph 30 below). The finding of a reasonable suspicion that the applicant had committed the offence was supported by the evidence of the second defendant, witness statements, forensic medical expert opinions, records of the seizure of a vehicle and information received from the Slovak authorities.

10.  The Buda Central District Court held that the applicant posed a risk of flight in view of the sentence of life imprisonment which could have been imposed on him. Noting that the facts established by the police included concealment of the offence following its commission in 2016, the District Court found it likely that the applicant would tamper with evidence, particularly that of persons involved in or having knowledge of the actions giving rise to the charges. It also took into account the applicant’s prior convictions by the Hungarian courts for misuse of explosives and firearms and by the Slovak courts for extortion and concluded that the applicant presented a risk of reoffending. In accordance with section 277 (4) a), b) and c) of the Code of Criminal Procedure (see paragraph 30 below), the District Court held that criminal supervision would not have been appropriate to mitigate the cumulative risks associated with the applicant.

11.  On 4 August 2020 the Budapest High Court dismissed the appeals of the prosecution, the applicant and his defence lawyer and upheld the decision and reasons of the District Court.

12.  On 25 August 2020 the District Court extended the applicant’s detention on the same grounds as those discussed in paragraphs 9 and 10 above. It also took into account that the proceeds of the crime, allegedly worth hundreds of thousands of euros (EUR), were still untraced, which it found to be a good reason for continuing to detain the applicant, because there was a risk he would abscond. It held that risks of the obstruction of proceedings and of his reoffending continued to be relevant and that criminal supervision could not be imposed on him at this early stage of the investigation. The High Court upheld that decision on 24 September 2020.

13.  On 25 November 2020 the District Court ordered the continued detention of the applicant on the same grounds. It also examined the timeliness of the investigation and concluded that the investigating authorities had taken several steps in the investigation as a matter of priority including, inter alia, the interrogation of the applicant, further hearings of witnesses, the appointment of a psychiatric expert, the use of a polygraph and various requests for information. It found that the risk of reoffending was supported by the most recent evidence of the applicant and the second defendant which had revealed that there were three criminal cases currently conducted against them in Slovakia. The High Court upheld that decision on 4 December 2020.

14.  On 22 January 2021 the District Court again ordered the continued detention of the applicant, for the same reasons as before. The applicant’s defence lawyer filed an appeal containing declarations of intent in regard to providing accommodation for the applicant, signed by his relatives, and he stated that they were ready to pay a surety of 20 million Hungarian forints (HUF, approximately EUR 55,000 at the time) so the applicant could be placed under criminal supervision although he had no residence of his own in Hungary. The High Court upheld the first-instance decision on 28 January 2021. It held in relation to the declarations appended to the appeal that they could not mitigate the risk of absconding that the applicant presented without any information certifying, in Hungarian, the relatives’ material circumstances.

15.  On 22 April 2021 the District Court again ordered the continued detention of the applicant for the same reasons. For the first time, the decision included a description of the weapon allegedly used by the applicant. It was also confirmed that the joint investigation team (see paragraph 6 above) had succeeded in recovering part of the proceeds of crime and were awaiting follow-up steps which had to be taken by the Slovak authorities. Official translations had been received about the continuing criminal proceedings in Slovakia, and the Hungarian police had conducted a site inspection of the crime scene and a reconstruction of the crime in an attempt to dispel confusion between the narratives of the defendants and the rest of the evidence. The District Court further clarified that forensic expert opinions were needed in four different areas of expertise. It observed that the applicant had continued to maintain contact with his parents and a sibling while in prison in Budapest and that there was no other measure which would have counterbalanced the risk of collusion, given that the applicant would have had access to a telephone and the opportunity to interact with others offline and online had he been put under criminal supervision. It took the view that the public interest that underlay the cross‑border investigation should prevail over the applicant’s right to be released pending trial. The High Court upheld that decision on 27 April 2021.

16.  The District Court again extended the applicant’s detention on 22 July 2021. It referred to further charges of causing grievous bodily harm (section 164 (1) and (3) of the Criminal Code) and attempted vandalism (section 371 (1) and (5) of the Criminal Code) allegedly committed by the applicant in 2015 and of which he had been notified by the police before the hearing. The District Court first examined the risk of flight, noting, inter alia, that the applicant was a single man without children and that he had parents and a sibling in the Slovak Republic who had been running his business in his absence. These circumstances were however not considered strong enough to remove the risk of his absconding, given the gravity of the charges against him and given that the authorities had been unable to trace the proceeds of the crime. Since the prosecution’s application for the continued detention of the applicant did not include any reference to a risk of obstruction of the proceedings, the District Court went on to examine the second ground, namely, the risk of reoffending. It found that ground established in view of the applicant’s criminal record, the criminal cases which were by then being heard with the homicide case and the psychological expert report which described him as prone to antisocial, aggressive and manipulative behaviour. The Budapest High Court upheld the District Court’s decision on 30 July 2021.

17.  The District Court made further orders for the applicant’s continued detention on 25 August and 22 October 2021, which were upheld on appeal on 16 September and 29 October 2021, respectively.

18.  On 21 December 2021, the District Court extended the detention of the applicant, finding that he continued to present risks of absconding, obstruction of justice and reoffending. It noted that the prison services had reported that the applicant had threatened to kill one of the witnesses in his case. Another criminal investigation, concerning the charge of preparing to commit homicide, was started by the police on 9 November 2021. The District Court drew from the new information the conclusion that the applicant might obstruct the criminal proceedings by threatening or influencing potential witnesses and further concluded for the same reason that criminal supervision would not be appropriate. The High Court upheld that decision on 27 December 2021.

19.  The District Court again extended the applicant’s detention on 24 February 2022. In that decision, the District Court held that it was not relevant to its assessment of the risk of flight that the applicant was a foreign national and had no fixed address in Hungary. The court also held that the European Arrest Warrant (see paragraph 7 above) was irrelevant since the authorities had had full knowledge of the applicant’s address in the Slovak Republic since the beginning of the investigation. It held that the applicant continued to present a risk of absconding given the gravity of the offences, his criminal history, his motives and his record. The District Court took note of the completion of the investigation and also of the recent police discontinuance of his prosecution for the offence of preparation for homicide (see paragraph 18 above), as there was insufficient supporting evidence. Since the investigation was over, the District Court accepted that there was no longer any risk that the applicant would obstruct those proceedings. It also held, however, that continued detention was justified because of the risk that the applicant would commit further offences, given his criminal history and the forensic psychologist and psychiatrist expert opinions which had showed him to be inclined towards criminal behaviour (see paragraph 16 above).

20.  On 2 March 2022 the High Court upheld the decision. It held however that the fact that the applicant had no address, property or family of his own in Hungary indicated that there was a risk of flight and that the applicant’s Slovak nationality and residence had no impact on this finding. It dismissed an appeal by the prosecution and upheld the finding of the District Court that the applicant no longer presented any risk of obstructing proceedings because the investigation had been concluded and any attempt by the applicant to tamper with witnesses would not affect the trial given that the witnesses had already recorded their statements. The court concluded that if the applicant were allowed out on bail, even the strictest electronically supervised form of criminal supervision would not properly mitigate the multiple risks he presented.

21.  The District Court continued to uphold the applicant’s detention on 21 April 2022, justifying that decision by reference to the risks of absconding and further offending. It dismissed applications by the defence for the release of the applicant on condition that he reside at his address in Slovakia. The District Court ordered the applicant to be held in pre-trial detention because his criminal history and the unfavourable conclusions drawn by the forensic experts as to his behaviour and attitudes strongly suggested that he would not abide by the rules of criminal supervision in the Slovak Republic. The High Court upheld that decision on 27 April 2022.

22.  On 22 May 2022 the Central Investigating Prosecutor’s Office indicted the applicant and two other defendants for homicide committed against multiple persons with premeditation and for gain, as a joint offender (section 160 (1) and (2)(a)(b) and (f) of the Criminal Code); for two counts of causing grievous bodily harm as a principal (section 164 (1) and (3) of the Criminal Code); and for one count of attempted vandalism as a principal (section 371 (1) and (5) of the Criminal Code). The investigation file transmitted with the indictment had more than 20,000 pages, including the official records of steps taken in the investigation, classified information, operational information exchanged via the European Police Office (Europol), the results of cell site analysis of data records, various data transmitted by the Slovak authorities, nine forensic expert reports, forty witness statements and the statements of the applicant and the second defendant in the case.

23.  In the course of the preparation for trial, on 22 June 2022, the Budapest High Court (the trial judge) decided to extend the applicant’s detention until the pronouncement of the judgment of the court of first instance, under section 276 (2)(a)(ab) and (c)(cb) and section 277 (4)(a),(c) and (e) of the Code of Criminal Procedure (see paragraph 30 below). The court found that there was a risk of the applicant absconding, given the gravity of the offences, the severity of the potential sentence of life imprisonment, the circumstances of the offence, the psychologist’s report, the applicant’s lack of connection with Hungary and his association with known criminals. It further held that the applicant’s domestic and foreign convictions and the psychologist’s report showed that there was a risk of reoffending. His criminal history and the characterisation of him as being inclined towards criminal behaviour led the court to conclude that he could not be expected to comply with the rules of any less restrictive measure other than pre‑trial detention. The Budapest Court of Appeal upheld that decision on 19 July 2022.

24.  The Budapest High Court held hearings in the applicant’s case on 5 and 25 October, 9 and 15 December 2022.

25.  On 16 December 2022 the Budapest High Court carried out a review of the grounds of the applicant’s continued detention under section 291 (1)(a) of the Code of Criminal Procedure (see paragraph 30 below) and came to the same conclusion on the same grounds as in its decision of 22 June 2022 (see paragraph 23 above). The Budapest Court of Appeal upheld that decision on 2 February 2023. It also held that the finding of a risk of reoffending was justified by information about the applicant living a life of crime. It agreed with the District Court that no alternative measure would suffice since the applicant had so far shown no interest in observing the law voluntarily and because a restraining order would not have averted the risk of his absconding.

26.  The High Court held fifteen hearings in the applicant’s case in 2023, another fifteen hearings in 2024 and six hearings in 2025.

27.  On 18 July 2023, 12 February and 1 October 2024 the Budapest Court of Appeal again reviewed the grounds for the applicant’s continued detention at the statutory intervals, in accordance with section 291 (1)(b) and (c) of the Code of Criminal Procedure (see paragraph 30 below), coming to the same conclusions and on the same grounds as in its decision of 2 February 2023 (see paragraph 25 above). On 18 July 2023 it also ruled out the possibility of the applicant being released under criminal supervision to live at his registered address in the Slovak Republic because of his criminal record and the limited opportunity for police oversight. On 12 February 2024 the Court of Appeal likewise observed that there had been no substantial change imposing the applicant’s release and that there was still a risk of absconding and of reoffending. That decision was upheld by the Kúria on 10 April 2024.

28.  In its decision of 1 October 2024, the Court of Appeal held that there had not been any change of circumstances since its decision of 12 February 2024 when it had reviewed the reasonableness of the applicant’s detention. It held that the risk of absconding was corroborated by the gravity of the charges, the severity of the potential sentence (there was a possibility of a life sentence), the applicant’s lack of any personal or business attachment with Hungary and his criminal connections abroad. The Court of Appeal also held that there was a possibility of reoffending in view of the applicant’s criminal history (he had previous convictions in Hungary and Slovakia for violent offences) and the evidence of the expert psychologist, who had assessed the applicant as having a tendency to engage in repeated criminal behaviour. Furthermore, the Court of Appeal addressed the passage of more than four years since the applicant had been first remanded in detention (see paragraph 9 above). It held that the reasons for ordering the continued pre‑trial detention of the applicant had neither become less pressing nor ceased to be relevant. It added that the public interest in the successful conduct of the proceedings, the determination of the criminal charges and the enforcement of any sentence if he were convicted carried much greater weight than the applicant’s right to respect for his personal freedom.

29.  On 2 April 2025 the Budapest High Court convicted the applicant as charged and sentenced him to life imprisonment with no possibility of parole and 10 years of exclusion from participating in public affairs.

RELEVANT LEGAL FRAMEWORK AND PRACTICE

30.  The Code of Criminal Procedure provides as follows:

Section 271

“(1) When a coercive measure is ordered or enforced, efforts shall be made to ensure that the application of the coercive measure leads to the restriction of the fundamental rights of the person concerned only to the extent and for the time strictly necessary.

(2) A more restrictive coercive measure may be ordered if the objective of the coercive measure cannot be achieved by applying a less restrictive coercive measure or by any other step. ...”

Section 276

“(1) In proceedings for a criminal offence punishable by imprisonment, a coercive measure affecting personal freedom subject to judicial confirmation may be ordered, extended, or maintained against the defendant if

a) the defendant is reasonably suspected of having committed a criminal offence, or he was indicted, and

b) doing so is necessary to achieve the objective of the coercive measure affecting personal freedom subject to judicial confirmation, and that objective cannot be achieved by any other means.

(2) A coercive measure affecting personal freedom subject to judicial confirmation may be ordered in order to

a) ensure the attendance of a defendant if

aa) he has previously escaped, attempted to escape, or hidden from the court, the prosecution service, or an investigating authority, or

ab) it is reasonable to assume that he would become unavailable to a criminal process in particular by escaping or hiding,

b) prevent the complication or frustration of the taking of evidence if

ba) the defendant, with a view to frustrating the taking of evidence, has intimidated or illegally influenced a person involved in the criminal proceeding or any other person, or destroyed, falsified, or hidden any means of physical evidence, electronic data, or object subject to the forfeiture of assets, or

bb) it is reasonable to believe that the defendant would jeopardise the taking of evidence in particular by intimidating or illegally influencing a person involved in the criminal proceedings or any other person, or by destroying, falsifying, or hiding any means of physical evidence, electronic data, or object subject to the forfeiture of assets,

c) eliminate the possibility of reoffending if

ca) the defendant has continued the criminal offence which is the subject matter of the proceedings after he was interrogated as a suspect, or he has been interrogated as a suspect regarding any other intentional criminal offence punishable by imprisonment that was committed after he was interrogated as a suspect, or

cb) it is reasonable to believe that the defendant would complete the criminal offence he attempted or prepared, continue the criminal offence which is the subject matter of the proceedings, or commit another criminal offence punishable by imprisonment.”

Section 277

“(1) A restraining order may be issued to avoid the hindrance or frustration of the taking of evidence, or to eliminate the possibility of reoffending against the aggrieved party.

(2) Criminal supervision may be ordered to ensure the attendance of a defendant, avoid the hindrance or frustration of the taking of evidence, or eliminate the possibility of reoffending.

(3) Criminal supervision may be ordered in combination with making a restraining order.

(4) Pre-trial detention may be ordered to ensure the attendance of a defendant, avoid the hindrance or frustration of the taking of evidence, or eliminate the possibility of reoffending if, taking into account in particular

a) the nature of the criminal offence,

b) the progress and requirements of the investigation,

c) the personal and family situation of the defendant,

d) the relationship between the defendant and any other person involved in the criminal proceedings or any other person,

e) the behaviour of the defendant before and during the criminal proceedings,

the objectives of the coercive measure affecting the defendant’s personal freedom subject to judicial confirmation cannot be achieved by making a restraining order or by an order for criminal supervision. ...”

Section 291

“(1) After a bill of indictment has been issued, there shall be a review of whether the restraining order or the order for criminal supervision was necessary

a) by the trial court if there has been no determination and six months have passed since the trial court first made or extended the restraining order or the order for criminal supervision,

b) by the appeal court if the trial court has not yet determined the case and a year has passed since the trial court first made or extended the first restraining order or the first order for criminal supervision,

c) after the time for the review by the appeal court set out in point b), by the appeal court at least every six months, until the trial court determines the case.”

Section 298

“(1) The pre-trial detention may last up to

...

e) five years if the proceedings against the defendant are for a criminal offence punishable by life imprisonment.

...

(4) The maximum length of the pre-trial detention under paragraph (1) e) shall be extended by another year if

...

d) indictment was for the offence of homicide committed with premeditation, for gain, against multiple persons or as set out in section 160 (2) l), having regard to paragraph (7) a), of the Criminal Code, ....

(5) If the court orders criminal supervision solely because the maximum length of pre‑trial detention under paragraph (1) e) has been reached, then the court

a) shall require that the defendant may not leave a specific residence, other premises, or a fenced area without permission,

b) shall require a defendant whose place of residence is not suitable for criminal supervision to spend the period of criminal supervision at an accommodation provided by the State,

c) may not permit the defendant to leave the place designated for him in order to go to work.”

31.  The Constitutional Court examined the request of the Commissioner for Fundamental Rights for a review of the constitutionality of section 298 (2)(a) of the Code of Criminal Procedure (see paragraph 30 above). This rule provided that, in the case of prosecution for the most serious offences (punishable by life imprisonment), there was no upper limit on the duration of pre-trial detention. The Constitutional Court declared the contested provision unconstitutional in its decision no. 10/2021. (IV.7.) AB with effect from 30 September 2021. In the Constitutional Court’s view, the failure of the first-instance courts to deliver a decision in reasonable time in criminal cases where the defendant is held in detention is often not attributable to the defendant, who should, as a constitutional principle, not bear the consequences of judicial delays. It held that after the expiry of the maximum duration foreseen by the Code of Criminal Procedure for pre‑trial detention, strict measures of criminal supervision (including the use of electronic monitoring devices) should suffice. The Constitutional Court, declined, however, to specify a maximum period.

full_case_text_no_verdict:
THIRD SECTION

CASE OF HOXHA AND OTHERS v. ALBANIA

(Application no. 5805/23)













JUDGMENT


STRASBOURG

13 October 2026





This judgment is final but it may be subject to editorial revision.

In the case of Hoxha and Others v. Albania,

The European Court of Human Rights (Third Section), sitting as a Committee composed of:

Diana Kovatcheva, President,
Darian Pavli,
Vasilka Sancin, judges,
and Olga Chernishova, Deputy Section Registrar,

Having regard to:

the application (no. 5805/23) against the Republic of Albania lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) on 31 January 2023 by ten Albanian nationals (“the applicants”), whose relevant details are listed in the appended table, and who were represented by Mr E. Syziu, a lawyer practising in Tirana;

the decision to give notice of the complaint concerning access to a court to the Albanian Government (“the Government”), represented by Mr O. Moçka, General State Advocate;

the parties’ observations;

Having deliberated in private on 22 September 2026,

Delivers the following judgment, which was adopted on that date:

SUBJECT MATTER OF THE CASE

THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE

1.  The case concerns an alleged violation of the applicants’ right of access to the Supreme Court.

2.  On 2 September 1995 the Commission for the Restitution and Compensation of Property (“the Commission”) recognised the applicants’ inherited property rights on a plot measuring 5,878 sq. m situated in Tirana. It decided to restore part of that plot measuring 2,999.6 sq. m and to award compensation for 2,501.4 sq. m in one of the ways provided for by law. It further awarded the applicants the right to first refusal of a plot of 615 sq.m. In 1996 the title to the restored property was entered in the land register. The reasoning of the 1995 Commission decision expressly stated that the property had an actual surface area of 7,600 sq. m.

3.  On 12 September 2007 the Immovable Property Registration Office of Tirana (“the IPRO”) informed the applicants that because of an inconsistency between the plot restored under the decision and the accompanying map, it was unable to take any further action in respect of their property. On 12 March 2008 the applicants requested the Agency for the Restitution and Compensation of Property (“the Agency” - the successor of the Commission) to correct that inconsistency.

4.  On 18 March 2008 the Agency informed the applicants that they should submit a request for the correction of the Commission’s decision to the Agency’s Regional Office for the Restitution and Compensation of Property (“the regional office”) in accordance with Article 120 of the Code of Administrative Procedure.

5.  On 4 April 2008 the applicants submitted a request to the regional office for the rectification of the 1995 decision. On 14 November 2008 the regional office dismissed that request for lack of jurisdiction. It also indicated that under section 18 of the Property Act, the power to amend the Commission’s decision of 1995 rested with the Agency.

6.  On 25 November 2008 the applicants addressed the Agency’s central office (“the central office”), seeking the correction of the 1995 Commission’s decision. The proceedings before it lasted for more than three years because they were suspended pending the Constitutional Court’s decisions of 2010 and 2011 (see paragraph 15 below).

7.  On 7 November 2011 the Agency held that the Commission’s decisions were no longer subject to administrative review because the Agency lacked jurisdiction, as those decisions were considered quasi-judicial. It further noted that the 2008 decision of the regional office had been lawful, since at the time the request was lodged, the Agency’s central office had had the power to review decisions of former commissions. However, that jurisdiction had been removed following a ruling of the Constitutional Court in 2010.

8.  Following that response, the applicants brought a civil action in the Tirana District Court (“the District Court”), seeking the quashing of the Agency’s decision and the rectification of the 1995 Commission’s decision. On 3 December 2012 that court partly allowed the applicants’ claim. Relying on an expert report, it found that the documents establishing the applicants’ ancestor’s property rights referred to an outdated unit of measurement. It therefore ordered the rectification of the Commission’s decision of 1995 by adding the word “old” to the unit of measurement used in the operative part of that decision.

9.  The Agency and the State Advocate’s office appealed against that decision, arguing, inter alia, that the claim should be dismissed as time‑barred.

10.  On 26 June 2014 the Tirana Court of Appeal upheld the District Court’s judgment. The correction was entered in the land register.

11.  On 6 April 2022 the Supreme Court reversed in camera the lower courts’ judgment and dismissed the applicants’ claim as time-barred. It held that the applicants should have brought proceedings within 30 days of becoming aware of the discrepancy between the 1995 decision and the accompanying map. The Supreme Court held that even assuming that the applicants had not been aware of the inconsistency in 1995, the 30-day time‑limit to address the courts had started to run from the moment the IPRO had informed them of its existence. It further found that rather than lodging an administrative complaint, the applicants should have brought the matter directly before the domestic courts.

12.  On 12 October 2022 the Constitutional Court dismissed a constitutional complaint lodged by the applicants, on the grounds that it was of a fourth-instance nature.

RELEVANT DOMESTIC LAW AND PRACTICE

13.  Article 120 of the Code of Administrative Procedure provides that if an administrative act is valid but is found to contain inaccuracies or obvious errors, the competent authority may, either of its own motion or at the request of a party to the proceedings, correct any clerical errors or manifest inaccuracies in the act without altering its substance. Such corrections are not subject to any statutory time-limit.

14.  Section 18 of the 2004 Property Act, as amended by law no. 9684/2007, provided at the material time that, in respect of appeals against decisions given by the former local commissions recognising property rights or ordering the restitution of or compensation for property, both the expropriated party and the State Advocate’s office were entitled to lodge an appeal with the central office of the Agency. The expropriated party could subsequently appeal against that decision to the Tirana District Court within 30 days of its notification.

15.  An overview of the relevant domestic constitutional case-law is presented in Gaba v. Albania (no. 33369/17, §§ 51-56, 17 December 2024).

case_name: CASE OF ZOUVELOS AND OTHERS v. GREECE
full_case_text_no_verdict:
THIRD SECTION

CASE OF ZOUVELOS AND OTHERS v. GREECE

(Application no. 42800/18)













JUDGMENT


STRASBOURG

20 October 2026



This judgment is final but it may be subject to editorial revision.

In the case of Zouvelos and Others v. Greece,

The European Court of Human Rights (Third Section), sitting as a Committee composed of:

Peeter Roosma, President,
Ioannis Ktistakis,
Lətif Hüseynov, judges,
and Olga Chernishova, Deputy Section Registrar,

Having regard to:

the application (no. 42800/18) against the Hellenic Republic lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) on 31 August 2018 by five Greek nationals (“the applicants”), whose relevant details are listed in the appended table, who were represented by Ms K. Gouvitsa, a lawyer practising in Amaliada;

the decision to give notice of the complaints concerning Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention to the Greek Government (“the Government”), represented by their Agent, Ms N. Marioli, President of the State Legal Council, and their Agent’s delegate, Ms S. Papaioannou, Senior Advisor at the State Legal Council, and to declare the remainder of the application inadmissible;

the parties’ observations;

Having deliberated in private on 29 September 2026,

Delivers the following judgment, which was adopted on that date:

SUBJECT MATTER OF THE CASE

1.  The application concerns the amount of compensation payable to the applicants following the expropriation of their properties.

2.  By a joint ministerial decision issued on 11 February 2008 and published in the Official Government Gazette on 25 February 2008, the expropriation of the applicants’ properties, located in Amaliada, was ordered for the construction of a highway.

3.  On 24 February 2009 the Greek State lodged an application for the determination of the provisional compensation payable to the applicants.

4.  Hearings took place on 15, 29 and 30 October 2009.

5.  By judgment no. 53/2010 of 26 April 2010, the Amaliada Court of First Instance determined the provisional unitary amounts of compensation payable to the applicants as follows: 10.08 euros (EUR) per sq. m for plot no. 201 and EUR 5.42 per sq. m for plot no. 206 belonging to the first applicant; EUR 4.74 per sq. m for plot no. 300 and EUR 4.50 per sq. m for plot no. 305 belonging to the second applicant; EUR 101.08 per sq. m for plot no.078 belonging to the third applicant; EUR 101.08 per sq. m for plot no. 079 belonging to the fourth applicant; and EUR 4.74 per sq. m for plots nos. 316 and 318 and EUR 4.28 per sq. m for plot no. 321 belonging to the fifth applicant. The calculation was based on the values of the properties on the dates of the hearings before the first-instance court.

6.  The Amaliada Court of First Instance further held that the non-expropriated part of the properties would derive a special benefit from the execution of the works, as they would have access to the highway.

7.  On 20 October 2010 the Greek State lodged an application for the determination of the final compensation payable to the applicants.

8.  After two adjournments, on 12 May 2011 and 21 March 2013, the hearing took place on 15 January 2015.

9.  The applicants responded by taking the following legal actions. On 19 January 2011 the first applicant lodged a counterclaim seeking the determination of the final compensation and challenging the presumption that his remaining, non-expropriated properties would benefit from the execution of the works and submitted a written request to intervene in the proceedings. In addition, the first, second and fifth applicants challenged the presumption of benefit by orally requesting leave to intervene in the proceedings at the hearing held on 15 January 2015. The third and fourth applicants challenged the presumption of benefit by way of written submissions filed in the hearing of 15 January 2015. Lastly, on 14 October 2010 the fifth applicant lodged a separate application seeking the determination of the final compensation and challenging the presumption of benefit.

10.  By judgment no. 78/2016 of 31 May 2016, the Patras Court of Appeal dismissed as inadmissible the applicants’ claims as regards the presumption of benefit. In particular, it held that the first applicant had failed to comply with the provisions of Article 33 § 7 of Law no. 2971/2001, which set out that the presumption of benefit could be challenged within a time-limit of six months from the date of determination of provisional compensation (which, in the case at hand, had occurred on 26 April 2010; see paragraph 5 above). It further held that the oral requests by the first, second and fifth applicants to intervene in the proceedings and the written submissions of the third and fourth applicants had been aimed at extending the scope of the application for the determination of the final compensation, contrary to national procedural rules. Lastly, it held that the fifth applicant’s claims lacked factual details as to the parts of his properties to which the presumption of benefit had been applied.

11.  Furthermore, the Patras Court of Appeal determined the final unitary amounts of compensation payable to the applicants as follows: EUR 8 per sq. m for plot no. 201 and EUR 2.60 per sq. m for plot no. 206 belonging to the first applicant; EUR 2 per sq. m for plots nos. 300 and 305 belonging to the second applicant; EUR 6.50 per sq. m for plot no. 078 belonging to the third applicant; EUR 6.50 per sq. m for plot no. 079 belonging to the fourth applicant; and EUR 2.50 per sq. m for plots nos. 316, 318 and 350 and EUR 2 per sq. m for plot no. 321 belonging to the fifth applicant. It based its judgment on Article 17 § 2 (c) of the Greek Constitution and Article 13 § 1 (b) of Law no. 2882/2001, which set out that the final compensation should be calculated on the basis of the values of the expropriated properties on the date of the hearing before the appellate court (15 January 2015 in the case at hand), where more than one year has passed from the date of the hearing concerning the provisional compensation. It further based its judgment on the depreciation of property values from 2009 onward. As regards plots nos. 078 and 079, they had been recorded as lying within the settlement boundaries, an error that had subsequently been rectified, thus aligning their unit prices with the remainder of the plots in question.

12.  The applicants lodged an appeal on points of law, complaining that the appellate court had taken the date of the hearing before it, rather than the date of the hearing on the determination of the provisional compensation, as the critical date for determining the final compensation, resulting in lower amounts awarded to them. They further argued that the appellate court had erred in dismissing as inadmissible their claims regarding the presumption of benefit.

13.  The Court of Cassation examined the applicants’ arguments on the merits and dismissed them by way of judgment no. 2062/2017, which became final on 1 March 2018. With respect to the critical date for determining the final compensation, the Court of Cassation ruled that Article 17 § 2 (c) of the Greek Constitution and Article 13 § 1 (b) of Law no. 2882/2001 applied regardless of any increase or decrease in property values occurring between the hearing in respect of the provisional compensation and that in respect of the final compensation. With respect to the applicants’ claims challenging the presumption of benefit, the Court of Cassation upheld the findings of the appellate court and further held that, in any event, all of the applicants’ claims lacked sufficient factual details concerning the parts of their properties which, allegedly, would not benefit from the execution of the works.

14.  The applicants complained of a violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention, reiterating the arguments they had made before the domestic courts.
