case_name: CASE OF FIŠIĆ v. CROATIA
full_case_text_no_verdict:
FIRST SECTION

CASE OF FIŠIĆ v. CROATIA

(Application no. 18788/22)





JUDGMENTSTRASBOURG

29 October 2026



This judgment will become final in the circumstances set out in Article 44 § 2 of the Convention. It may be subject to editorial revision.

In the case of Fišić v. Croatia,

The European Court of Human Rights (First Section), sitting as a Chamber composed of:

Erik Wennerström, President,
Raffaele Sabato,
Frédéric Krenc,
Davor Derenčinović,
Alain Chablais,
Artūrs Kučs,
Anna Adamska-Gallant, judges,
and Liv Tigerstedt, Deputy Section Registrar,

Having regard to:

the application (no. 18788/22) against the Republic of Croatia lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a Croatian national, Mr Oliver Fišić (“the applicant”), on 6 April 2022;

the decision to give notice to the Croatian Government (“the Government”) of the complaint concerning access to a court and to declare the remainder of the application inadmissible;

the parties’ observations;

Having deliberated in private on 6 October 2026,

Delivers the following judgment, which was adopted on that date:

INTRODUCTION

1.  The case concerns the applicant’s complaint under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention that he had been denied access to a tribunal to defend his rights in relation to a mayoral decision adopted in a public tender procedure in which he had participated as a bidder.

THE FACTS

2.  The applicant was born in 1968 and lives in Brašina. He was represented by Mr B. Radan, a lawyer practising in Zagreb.

3.  The Government were represented by their Agent, Ms Š. Stažnik.

4.  The facts of the case may be summarised as follows.

CALL FOR TENDERS FOR THE LEASE OF PUBLIC AREAS IN THE MUNICIPALITY OF ŽUPA DUBROVAČKA

5.  On 15 March 2017 the mayor of Župa dubrovačka ordered a municipal committee to organise a call for tenders for the lease of certain of the municipality’s public areas, to be used, inter alia, for vending stands.

6.  The tender, which was published on 20 March 2017, set out the eligibility criteria, the lease duration, minimum bid amounts and the deadline for submissions.

It also stated that the best bidder would be selected in accordance with the municipality of Župa dubrovačka’s decision on the lease of public areas (“the municipality’s Decision”, see paragraph 24 below).

7.  The applicant submitted a bid of 16 Croatian kunas (HRK) per square metre per day for a vending stand in Brašina. Another bidder, N.P., submitted a bid of HRK 11 per square metre per day for the same location.

8.  On 5 April 2017 the committee found that both bids had been submitted on time and complied with the specifications. As the bids differed, it decided under section 13 of the municipality’s Decision (see paragraph 24 below) that N.P., as the previous lessee, would be offered the lease at the higher price submitted by the applicant. On 21 April 2017 N.P. agreed to pay the higher price.

9.  On 26 April 2017 the mayor accepted N.P.’s bid and concluded a lease agreement with her.

10.  The applicant lodged an objection, arguing that the mayoral decision had been unlawful. On 27 July 2017 the Municipal Council dismissed the objection, emphasising that section 13 of the municipality’s Decision granted priority to the previous lessee in order to ensure legal certainty for entrepreneurs.

11.  On 28 July 2017 the municipality, represented by the mayor, concluded a lease agreement with N.P.

PROCEEDINGS IN THE ADMINISTRATIVE COURTS

12.  The applicant brought an administrative action in the Split Administrative Court (Upravni sud u Splitu), challenging the mayoral decision of 26 April 2017. He argued that the misapplication of section 13 of the municipality’s Decision had placed him at a disadvantage vis-à-vis the other tenderer, whose bid was lower than his. He submitted that priority ought to be given to the previous lessee only if two identical bids were submitted, which had not been the case. Moreover, section 13 did not provide for the possibility for the previous lessee to have disclosed or match the highest bid.

13.  On 9 April 2019 the Split Administrative Court set aside the Municipal Council’s decision of 27 July 2017 (see paragraph 10 above) but upheld the mayoral decision of 26 April 2017 (see paragraph 9 above).

It noted that, pursuant to a practice direction adopted by the Administrative Court of the Republic of Croatia on 28 April 2008 (see paragraph 25 below), acts granting the lease of public areas constituted administrative acts – that is, individual acts by which the public authority decided on the rights, obligations or legal interests of an individual in an administrative matter (see paragraph 21 below). Such decisions were therefore subject to a review of their lawfulness in administrative disputes where the administrative courts applied the Constitution and the relevant statutory law.

The Split Administrative Court further noted that the legislation did not allow for the lodging of an appeal against individual mayoral acts deciding on the rights, obligations and legal interests of an individual. Such decisions could instead be challenged in an administrative court. For that reason, the Split Administrative Court concluded that the Municipal Council had lacked competence to review the mayoral decision and, accordingly, set aside its decision of 27 July 2017.

It reviewed the lawfulness of the mayoral decision of 26 April 2017 and concluded that the facts had been properly established and that the relevant law had been properly applied.

14.  The applicant appealed against that judgment, reiterating the arguments set out in paragraph 12 above and adding that, had section 13 of the municipality’s Decision provided for the possibility of the previous lessee to have disclosed or match the highest bid, he would never have bothered to submit a bid in the first place.

15.  On 24 September 2020 the High Administrative Court quashed the Split Administrative Court’s judgment and declared the applicant’s administrative action inadmissible. It held that, pursuant to its decision of 26 January 2015 delivered in the context of a specific tender procedure (see paragraph 26 below), decisions on the lease of public areas did not constitute administrative acts but acts of property management and thus fell outside the scope of administrative judicial review.

CONSTITUTIONAL COURT PROCEEDINGS

16.  On 1 April 2021 the applicant lodged a constitutional complaint, alleging violations of his constitutional rights to a fair trial, equality before the law, and entrepreneurial and market freedom. He relied on the State’s obligation to ensure that all entrepreneurs had equal status on the market (see paragraph 19 below).

17.  On 22 December 2021 the Constitutional Court dismissed the complaint as manifestly ill-founded. It found that the restriction on the right of access to a court had been constitutionally acceptable, having regard to the sufficient and relevant reasons provided by the High Administrative Court.

18.  That decision was served on the applicant on 10 January 2022.

RELEVANT LEGAL FRAMEWORK AND PRACTICE
RELEVANT DOMESTIC LAW

19.  The relevant provisions of the Constitution (Ustav Republike Hrvatske, Official Gazette no. 56/1990, with subsequent amendments) read as follows:

Article 29 § 1

“Everyone shall be entitled to have his or her rights and obligations, or suspicion or accusation of a criminal offence, decided upon fairly and within a reasonable time by an independent and impartial court established by law.”

Article 49

“Entrepreneurial and market freedom are the foundations of the economic system of the Republic of Croatia.

The State shall ensure that all entrepreneurs have equal legal status on the market. The abuse of monopolies, as determined by law, is prohibited.

...”

20.  The relevant provision of the Trade Act (Zakon o trgovini, Official Gazette no. 87/2008, with subsequent amendments) reads as follows:

Section 4(2)

“A trader shall carry out trading activities freely and under equal conditions on the market, in such a way that competition is neither prevented, restricted nor distorted.”



21.  The relevant provisions of the Administrative Disputes Act 2010 (Zakon o upravnim sporovima, Official Gazette no. 20/2010, with subsequent amendments), as in force during the proceedings instituted by the applicant in the administrative courts, read as follows:

Section 3

“(1)  The subject matter of an administrative dispute is:

1.  review of the lawfulness of an individual decision by which a public authority has decided on the right, obligation or legal interests of an individual in an administrative matter (an administrative act) against which no ordinary legal remedy is permitted;

2.  review of the lawfulness of the conduct of a public authority in the field of administrative law by which a right, obligation or the legal interests of an individual has been infringed, and against which no ordinary legal remedy is permitted;

3.  review of the lawfulness of a failure on the part of a public authority in the field of administrative law to decide, within the time-limit prescribed by law, on a right, obligation, legal interests or ordinary legal remedy of an individual, or to act in accordance with a regulation;

4.  review of the lawfulness of the conclusion, termination or fulfilment of an administrative contract.

...”

Section 4

“(1)  An administrative dispute may not be brought in matters for which judicial protection is provided outside of an administrative dispute.

(2)  An administrative dispute may not be brought concerning the correctness of an individual decision made at the discretion of a public authority, but it may be conducted concerning the lawfulness of such a decision, the limits of authority, and the purpose for which the authority was granted.

...”

Section 5

“In an administrative dispute, the court shall issue a decision on the basis of the Constitution and relevant statutory law.”

22.  The relevant provisions of the Ownership and Other Rights In Rem Act (Zakon o vlasništvu i drugim stvarnim pravima, Official Gazette no. 91/1996, with subsequent amendments – “the Property Act”) read as follows:

Section 35

“(1)  The Republic of Croatia and other legal persons governed by public law which hold ownership rights shall, as owners, have the same status in legal relations as private owners, unless otherwise provided by law.

(2)  Property owned by the Republic of Croatia shall be disposed of, administered and used by the Republic of Croatia’s government or by a body authorised by it, unless otherwise provided by a special law. Powers of disposal, administration and use in respect of property owned by local and regional self-government units shall be exercised by the bodies of those units as designated by the legislation governing the organisation of local and regional self-government units, unless otherwise provided by a special law.

...

(8)  The rules governing ownership by the Republic of Croatia shall apply, mutatis mutandis, to the ownership rights of local and regional self-government units, unless otherwise provided for by law or where required otherwise by the nature of those entities. ...”

Section 391

“(1)  Immovable property owned by local and regional self-government units may be alienated or otherwise disposed of by the competent authorities only on the basis of a public tender procedure and for compensation determined at market value, unless otherwise provided by law.

(2)  The provisions of paragraph 1 of this section shall not apply where the ownership of immovable property owned by local or regional self-government units is acquired by the Republic of Croatia, local or regional self-government units, or legal persons owned wholly or predominantly by the Republic of Croatia, or by legal persons owned wholly or predominantly by local or regional self-government units, where this serves the interest and objective of the general economic and social development of their citizens.

(3)   Land owned by local or regional self-government units may be sold by the competent authorities at a price determined by the market without organising a public tender procedure:

–  to a person to whom part of that land is necessary for the development of a vacant plot of land in accordance with a zoning permit or detailed land-use plan, provided that such land does not exceed 20% of the total area; and

...

(5)  Legal transactions concluded contrary to the provisions of this section shall be null and void.”

23.  The relevant provisions of the Local and Regional Self‑Government Act (Zakon o lokalnoj i područnoj (regionalnoj) samoupravi, Official Gazette, no. 33/2001, with subsequent amendments) read as follows:

Section 48

“(1)  The municipal mayor, city mayor, or county prefect:

...

manages immovable and movable property owned by the local or regional self‑government unit, together with related revenue and expenditure, in accordance with the relevant laws and regulations;

...”

Section 67

“(1)  The assets of a local or regional self-government unit shall include all movable and immovable property, and property rights.

(2)  A local or regional self-government unit must manage, use, and dispose of its assets with the diligence of a prudent manager.”

24.  The Decision on the lease of public areas in the municipality of Župa dubrovačka (Odluka o zakupu javnih površina Župe dubrovačke, Official Gazette of the municipality of Župa Dubrovačka nos. 1/2010 and 15/2013) set out the conditions and procedure for the lease of public areas within the municipality. It provided that “public areas” included land designated for general use in accordance with spatial planning documents (such as streets, squares, and public green areas), the management of which was entrusted to the mayor.

Section 9 of the Decision provided that the municipal mayor was to organise a public call for tenders specifying the key details of the lease, including the public area concerned, its intended use, the starting rent per square metre, the deposit, the deadline and procedure for submitting bids, the lease duration, and any other relevant conditions.

Section 12 of the Decision provided that the selection of the most favourable bidder in the public tender shall be made by the municipal mayor on the proposal of the municipal committee.

Section 13 of the Decision provided that, when selecting the most favourable bidder, the municipal mayor would give priority based on the following order: (1) lessees from the previous year who had duly fulfilled their contractual obligations; (2) Croatian disabled war veterans; (3) family members of Croatian war veterans who were killed in the war; (4) individuals employing such veterans or their family members on a permanent basis on the premises concerned; (5) individuals who had voluntarily joined the Croatian armed forces between 1991 and 1992; (6) members of the Croatian armed forces or police involved in the war for at least six consecutive months between 1991 and 1992; and (7) on an equal basis, persons with permanent residence in the municipality. Following a final decision on the selection of the most favourable bidder, a lease agreement was to be concluded.

DOMESTIC COURT PRACTICE

25.  On 28 April 2008 the Administrative Court of the Republic of Croatia (Upravni sud Republike Hrvatske)[1] adopted practice direction no. 7 Su‑618/08-3 which stipulated that “acts awarding the use of public areas” constituted administrative acts. Such acts were therefore subject to administrative judicial review.

26.  This approach changed in 2015. Specifically, in decision no. Usoz‑38/14-5 of 26 January 2015, delivered in the context of a tender procedure in which the mayor of Zagreb had granted a lease of immovable property to the Croatian Football Federation, the High Administrative Court held – without providing detailed reasoning – that the mayoral decision had not constituted an administrative act but rather an act of property management (raspolaganje imovinom). By decision no. U-III-1276/2015 of 14 November 2019 the Constitutional Court found that the High Administrative Court had given relevant and sufficient reasons for its conclusion and held that the complainant’s right of access to a court had not been violated.

27.  Following this shift, the administrative courts treated mayoral decisions granting the lease of property in tender procedures as acts of property management that were not subject to review, and declared related administrative actions inadmissible. That approach was applied in a line of cases between 2016 and 2020 concerning both decisions granting leases and decisions annulling tender procedures, and was regularly upheld on appeal.

28.  Accordingly, in the decisions of 25 March 2016 (Split Administrative Court, no. Usl-120/14-6, upheld by the High Administrative Court on 28 September 2016, no. Usž-2432/16-2), 11 June 2018 (Rijeka Administrative Court, no. Usl-607/18-2, upheld by the High Administrative Court on 30 August 2018, no. Usž-3293/18-2), and 4 November 2020 (High Administrative Court, no. Usž-1426/20-2), administrative actions against mayoral decisions awarding leases of business premises were declared inadmissible on the grounds that such decisions did not constitute administrative acts but rather acts of property management.

29.  The same reasoning was applied in various decisions annulling tender procedures. In the decisions of 24 April 2017 (Rijeka Administrative Court, no. UsI-499/17-3, upheld by the High Administrative Court on 1 March 2018, no. Usž-1964/17-2) and 30 November 2017 (Rijeka Administrative Court, no. UsI-1536/17-2, upheld by the High Administrative Court on 18 July 2018, no. Usž-157/2018-2), the courts held that such decisions constituted acts of property management and were not subject to review.

30.  In the latter line of cases, the Constitutional Court held, in its decision of 23 September 2020 (no. U-III-4030/2018), that judicial protection had to be ensured in respect of all individual acts by public authorities, regardless of their nature. It pointed out that all courts were under an obligation to safeguard the constitutional and Convention right to judicial protection, particularly when reviewing decisions of public authorities. It added that the courts had to ensure that all the parties had access to a court by interpreting the law purposively – that is, at a minimum, by directing them to another available form of effective legal protection or, if none existed, by explaining why judicial protection was not required.

31.  In a number of cases from 2018 onwards, the administrative courts reverted to their earlier position, again classifying decisions granting the use of public areas as administrative acts subject to administrative judicial review, in accordance with the 2008 practice direction (see paragraph 25 above). In those cases, the courts examined the merits and, where appropriate, set aside mayoral decisions for lack of reasoning or unlawfulness.

32.  For example, by judgment no. Usl-871/17-22 of 23 March 2018, the Rijeka Administrative Court held that, pursuant to the 2008 practice direction, a mayoral decision in a public tender granting the lease of a public area constituted an administrative decision and was as such amenable to judicial review. It set aside the decision, finding that it had lacked the required statutory elements, including the reasons for selecting the winning bid. By judgment no. Usž-3246/18-2 of 19 November 2020, the High Administrative Court upheld that judgment, emphasising that, if the reasons for selecting a bid were not provided, it was impossible to assess either the correctness of the established facts, or the lawfulness of the contested decision.

33.  By decision no. Usž-3307/17-2 of 13 December 2018, the High Administrative Court quashed a decision by the Split Administrative Court declaring inadmissible an administrative action to challenge a mayoral decision granting the lease of a public area in a public tender. Referring to the 2008 practice direction, it held that such decisions constituted administrative acts and ordered the lower court to examine the case on the merits.

34.  By decision no. Usž-4094/22-2 of 15 February 2023, the High Administrative Court quashed a decision by the Rijeka Administrative Court declaring inadmissible an administrative action against a mayoral decision, likewise relying on the 2008 practice direction.

35.  In the remitted proceedings, by judgment no. Usl-356/2023-7 of 5 September 2023 the Rijeka Administrative Court examined the case on the merits and set aside the mayoral decision. In the tender procedure at issue, the complainant had submitted the highest bid; however, another bidder had been given priority on the basis of local residency, invited to match the offer, and ultimately selected.

The Rijeka Administrative Court found that such preferential treatment on the basis of residence had directly conflicted with the principles of free‑market competition and the equal legal status of entrepreneurs guaranteed by Article 49 of the Croatian Constitution and set out in Article 4(2) of the Trade Act (cited at paragraphs 19 and 20 above). Those provisions stipulated that economic activity should be conducted freely and under equal market conditions, without any restrictions on or distortions to competition. By favouring “local” bidders, the contested decision had violated those principles.

It further clarified that although local authorities could grant preferential access to public services (such as childcare or social programmes) to their residents, this did not extend to economic activities. The lease of public areas for commercial purposes was not a public service but rather a means of facilitating private business. Municipalities therefore lacked authority to grant advantages to local entrepreneurs in this context.

The court further observed that the contested mechanism had created only an illusion of equality and although the highest bid appeared to be the decisive criterion, local bidders had been allowed to match competing offers after their disclosure, a privilege not afforded to others. This had conferred an unjust advantage, undermined genuine competition and had violated the requirement that all bidders were to compete on equal terms.

Lastly, the court held that the measure had been incompatible with EU law, in particular Directive 2006/123/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council of 12 December 2006 on services in the internal market (“the Bolkenstein Directive”), which prohibited discrimination on the basis of the location of the registered office and did not recognise residence as a valid overriding public-interest justification for restricting the freedom to provide services.

36.  By judgment no. Usž-2721/2023-2 of 10 July 2024, the High Administrative Court upheld that judgment.

case_name: CASE OF HÁTTÉR TÁRSASÁG AND AMNESTY INTERNATIONAL MAGYARORSZÁG v. HUNGARY
full_case_text_no_verdict:
SECOND SECTION

CASE OF HÁTTÉR TÁRSASÁG AND AMNESTY INTERNATIONAL MAGYARORSZÁG v. HUNGARY

(Application no. 43901/22)





JUDGMENTSTRASBOURG

3 November 2026





This judgment will become final in the circumstances set out in Article 44 § 2 of the Convention. It may be subject to editorial revision.



In the case of Háttér Társaság and Amnesty International Magyarország v. Hungary,

The European Court of Human Rights (Second Section), sitting as a Chamber composed of:

Arnfinn Bårdsen, President,
Jovan Ilievski,
Péter Paczolay,
Oddný Mjöll Arnardóttir,
Stéphane Pisani,
Juha Lavapuro,
Hugh Mercer, judges,
and Andrea Tamietti, Section Registrar,

Having regard to:

the application (no. 43901/22) against Hungary lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by two Hungarian organisations, Háttér Társaság (“the first applicant organisation”) and Amnesty International Hungary (“the second applicant organisation) (collectively “the applicant organisations”), on 22 August 2022;

the decision to give notice to the Hungarian Government (“the Government”) of the application;

the observations submitted by the respondent Government and the observations in reply submitted by the applicant organisations;

the comments submitted by the Helsinki Foundation for Human Rights, which was granted leave to intervene by the President of the Section;

Having deliberated in private on 6 October 2026,

Delivers the following judgment, which was adopted on that date:

INTRODUCTION

1.  The applicant organisations complain of a violation of their right to freedom of expression under Article 10 of the Convention and a violation of their right to a fair trial under Article 6 of the Convention arising from a decision of the National Election Commission (hereinafter, “the NEC”) imposing fines on them for calling on voters to cast invalid ballots in a national referendum.

THE FACTS

2.  The applicant organisations are based in Budapest. They were represented by Mr Tordai, a lawyer practising in Budapest.

3.  The Government were represented by their Agent, Mr Z. Tallódi, of the Ministry of Justice.

4.  The facts of the case may be summarised as follows.

BACKGROUND OF THE CASE

5.  In July 2021 the Hungarian Government organised a referendum, the stated aim of which was the protection of children’s best interests. They submitted the following questions to the NEC with a view to their being put to the people in the referendum: 1) “Do you agree with the idea of workshops presenting different sexual orientations being held for underage children in public education institutions, without the consent of their parents?” 2) “Do you agree with the promotion of gender reassignment surgeries to underage children?” 3) “Do you agree with the unrestricted exposure of underage children to sexually explicit media content that may influence their development?” 4) “Do you agree with the broadcasting of media content showing gender reassignment?” 5) “Do you agree with gender reassignment surgery being made accessible to underage children?”

6.  Following legal challenges, the President of the Republic announced that the referendum would be held on 3 April 2022 (“the 2022 Referendum”) and that it would include only the first four of the above-mentioned five questions.

7.   The applicant organisations, together with twelve other civil-society organisations, initiated a campaign encouraging voters to cast invalid ballots because they considered that the questions included in the referendum were misleading and promoted homophobic and transphobic policies.

8.  The referendum was held on 3 April 2022, on the same day as a general election. Approximately 1,700,000 voters casted an invalid ballot. The invalid votes constituted about 30% of the ballots cast. The results of the referendum were therefore invalid with respect to all four questions as the majority of all registered voters did not cast a valid vote.

PROCEEDINGS AGAINST THE APPLICANT ORGANISATIONS
Decisions of the NEC

9.  Following a complaint by a third party, the NEC found that the first applicant organisation, by publishing on its Facebook page posts calling on voters to cast an invalid ballot, had infringed the “principle of exercise of rights in accordance with their purpose” (rendeltetésszerű joggyakorlás) laid down in section 2(1)(e) of Act no. XXXVI of 2013 on Electoral Procedure (hereinafter, “the EPA”, see paragraph 24 below). In a decision of 8 April 2022 (no. 324/2022) the NEC ordered the first applicant organisation to pay a fine of 3,000,000 Hungarian forints (HUF – approximately 7,400 euros (EUR)). The NEC explained that voters had the right to cast invalid ballots, but that a campaign encouraging voters to do so was not compatible with the purposes of the referendum. It continued that the first applicant organisation’s campaign activity had not been aimed at encouraging people to express their will but rather at obstructing the purpose of the referendum, which was to allow the people to express their will as legislators.

10.  On the same day, also following a complaint by a third party, the NEC issued decision no. 328/2022 finding that the applicant organisations had operated the website ervenytelenul.hu (meaning “invalid”), which had contained a call on voters to “Cast an invalid vote in response to an invalid question”. The website had advised voters how to mark their ballots at the referendum such that they were invalid. For the same reasons as in decision no. 324/2022, the NEC found that the applicant organisations’ campaign activity had infringed section 2(1)(e) of the EPA and the “principle of the exercise of rights in accordance with their purpose”. The NEC did not find it necessary to impose a fine on the applicant organisations, as the campaign period had terminated.

Decisions of the Kúria

11.  The first applicant organisation sought judicial review of decision no. 342/2022 (see paragraph 9 above) before the Kúria. It pointed out that a referendum was a direct manifestation of popular sovereignty; consequently, the referendum campaigning period that preceded referendums served as a crucial forum for the discussion of public affairs. Encouraging voters to adopt a certain conduct in respect of a referendum fell within the most highly protected aspect of the right to freedom of expression, as recognised in Article IX § 1 of the Fundamental Law. The purpose of referendum campaigning was to influence voters regarding whether to participate in a referendum and how to vote. In the view of the first applicant organisation, encouraging voters to cast an invalid vote, which was their lawful choice, was not contrary to the purpose of the referendum campaigning period. Thus, its own conduct of encouraging the casting of invalid votes had not violated the purpose of the referendum campaigning period but remained strictly within its scope. The first applicant organisation argued that the contested NEC decision imposing a fine for the infringement of the principle of exercise of rights in accordance with their purpose was not in accordance with section 2(1)(e) of the EPA.

12.  In its decision no. Kvk.IV.39.419/2022/4 of 13 April 2022 the Kúria rejected the first applicant organisation’s claim for judicial review without an examination of the merits. It held that although the first applicant organisation had formally cited a fundamental principle set out in the EPA, it had failed to demonstrate the specific grounds for its contention that the NEC decision did not conform to that provision. It had not explained why section 2(1)(e) of the EPA could not be interpreted in the way the NEC had done. Furthermore, although the first applicant organisation had stated that the NEC decision had disregarded the fundamental rights aspect of the case, it had failed to lay out the precise interests, rights or constitutional values which it claimed the NEC had failed to balance, or to explain what it thought the outcome of such a balancing exercise should have been.

13.  The applicant organisations also sought judicial review of the NEC’s decision no. 328/2022 (see paragraph 10 above), including essentially the same reasoning as had been presented in the claim for judicial review lodged by the first applicant organisation (see paragraph 11 above). In addition, the applicant organisations submitted that the restriction of their campaign activity could only have been justified if there had been a specific statutory basis for doing so and if the restriction had been necessary and proportionate. However, no specific statutory provision prohibited encouraging the casting of an invalid vote, nor was such a prohibition strictly necessary to ensure the exercise of another fundamental right or to protect a constitutional value; consequently, section 2(1)(e) of the EPA could be interpreted in a manner consistent with the Fundamental Law that would not render campaign activity encouraging the casting of an invalid vote unlawful.

14.  In decision no. Kvk.IV.39.420/2022/4 of 13 April 2022 the Kúria dismissed the claim for judicial review, on the same grounds as in decision no. Kvk.IV.39.419/2022/4 (see paragraph 12 above).

Decisions of the Constitutional Court

15.   The applicant organisations each lodged constitutional complaints, arguing that the Kúria’s decisions had infringed their right to freedom of expression, as protected by Article IX of the Fundamental Law, and their right to a fair trial, as protected by Article XXVIII of the Fundamental Law. They submitted that the Kúria had failed to adjudicate the merits of their claims and had not addressed their arguments concerning their campaign promoting the casting of invalid ballots, thereby disregarding the fundamental-rights element of their claim. They reiterated that the NEC’s decision restricting their right to freedom of expression had no legal basis and had been disproportionate.

16.  The Constitutional Court rejected the complaints on 22 April 2022 (decisions nos. 3216/2022 (V.11)AB and 3217/2022 (V.11)AB) on the same grounds. As regards the complaint concerning the alleged infringement of the right to a fair trial, the Constitutional Court held that the complaints did not raise a constitutional issue but challenged the legality of the Kúria’s decision. The Constitutional Court dismissed the applicant organisations’ argument that the Kúria had reached different conclusions in cases similar to theirs, reasoning that the Kúria was bound by the content of the claim for judicial review and finding that no information had been submitted to substantiate the contention that the Kúria had ruled differently on claims that were identical in terms of form and substance. As regards the alleged violation of the right to freedom of expression, the Constitutional Court reasoned in essence that the legality of the NEC’s decision had not been examined by the Kúria for procedural reasons, and that an examination by the Kúria was a precondition for a constitutional review.

OTHER CASES BEFORE THE DOMESTIC AUTHORITIES

17.  On 8 April 2022 the NEC issued three other decisions.

18.  In decision no. 325/2022 the NEC fined the second applicant organisation HUF 3,000,000 (approximately EUR 7,400) for publishing Facebook posts calling on voters to cast invalid ballots, in breach of section 2(1)(e) of the EPA.

19.  Following a claim for judicial review lodged by the second applicant organisation, the Kúria overturned the NEC’s decision (decision no. Kvk.V.39.421/2022/5) on 15 April 2022, holding that campaign activities formed part of the freedom to express opinions on public affairs. They could only be restricted to in order to give effect to another fundamental right or to protect a constitutional value, and even then only to the extent strictly necessary, in proportion to the intended objective and while respecting the essential content of the fundamental right (see paragraph 25 below).

20.  In decision no. 327/2022 the NEC fined the applicant organisations and fourteen other civil-society organisations HUF 176,400 (approximately EUR 430) each for publishing on the website of the second applicant organisation a political announcement which the NEC considered to be in breach of the principle of exercise of rights in accordance with their purpose.

21.  The civil-society organisations lodged a claim for judicial review of the decision with the Kúria. On 15 April 2022 by decision no. Kvk.V.39.422/2022/3 the Kúria overturned the NEC’s decision, reasoning that in the event of a conflict between the fundamental principle that rights had to be exercised in good faith and in accordance with their purpose – as set forth in section 2(1)(e) of the EPA – and the fundamental right of voters to freedom of expression, the latter could not be restricted without a constitutional basis and a statutory mandate. The Kúria held that the claimants had taken a position on a matter of public interest regarding the casting of invalid votes in the referendum and had exercised their fundamental right to freedom of expression; that right could not be lawfully restricted on the grounds cited by the NEC (see paragraph 26 below).

22.  In decision no. 329/2020 the NEC held that a civil-society organisation, the Hungarian Civil Liberties Union, had breached section 2(1)(e) of the EPA by publishing on its website a call to “cast an invalid ballot in the Government’s discriminatory referendum!”. The NEC did not find it necessary to impose a fine on the organisation, as the campaign period had ended.

23.  In decision no. Kvk.VI.39.423/2022/6 of 15 April 2022, the Kúria overturned the NEC’s decision. The Kúria held that the exercise of the right to freedom of expression – guaranteed by the Fundamental Law – by the Civil Liberties Union during its campaign activity could not be classified as a violation of the fundamental principle set forth in section 2(1)(e) of the EPA in the absence of an explicit statutory restriction established with detailed reasoning by the NEC (see paragraph 27 below).

RELEVANT LEGAL FRAMEWORK AND PRACTICE

24.  The relevant domestic law is set out in the case of Magyar Kétfarkú Kutya Párt v. Hungary ([GC], no. 201/17, §§ 31-32, 20 January 2020). Additional relevant provisions of the EPA read as follow:

Judicial review

Section 222

“(1) A natural person, a legal entity or an organisation without legal personality affected by the case may submit a claim for judicial review against a second-instance decision of an election commission or a decision of the [NEC].

...”

Section 229

“(1)  The Kúria shall adjudicate such claims for judicial review.

(2)  The court shall decide on claims for judicial review in non-contentious proceedings, in a panel composed of five professional judges.

...”

Section 233

“(1) A constitutional complaint against a judicial decision – given pursuant to this Act in the context of a legal remedy concerning a decision of an election body – may be lodged with the Constitutional Court within three days of the handing down of the contested decision.

(2) The Constitutional Court shall decide on a constitutional complaint against a judicial decision – given pursuant to this Act in the context of a legal remedy concerning a decision of an election body – within five days of its receipt.

...”

25.  Decision no. Kvk.V.39.421/2022/5 of the Kúria (see paragraph 19 above) contains the following relevant passages:

“...

[53] In its decisions nos. 3313/2019 (XI. 21.) and 3279/2019 (XI. 5.), the Constitutional Court established that, pursuant to Article I § 3 of the Fundamental Law, the right to freedom of expression may only be restricted by an Act of Parliament; therefore, in the absence of an express statutory provision, the necessity of restricting a fundamental right cannot be established by judicial interpretation.

[54] Given that there is no statutory provision restricting or prohibiting the casting of an invalid vote or calling [on people] to do so – and considering that an invalid vote qualifies as a vote – the claimant’s campaign activity did not effectively infringe upon the essence of the referendum as defined by the Fundamental Law, nor did it affect the voting autonomy of citizens.

[55] Accordingly, in the view of the Kúria, the claimant’s freedom of speech – which enjoys a heightened level of protection during a campaign – cannot lawfully be restricted by invoking the purpose of the referendum.

[56] The Kúria has found that the [NEC] failed to recognise that the [case] involved a potential restriction of the claimant’s fundamental right to freedom of expression and thus failed to take into account that such a fundamental right may only be restricted in accordance with Article I § 3 of the Fundamental Law. Instead, it erroneously proceeded from the premise that the stage of the referendum process concerning the validation of questions requires examining whether an unequivocal answer can be given to the questions and whether the ballot paper excludes any third response option alongside “yes” and “no”. The objection concerned the referendum campaign rather than the validation stage; consequently, the criteria for its assessment necessarily differ. The decision of the [NEC] – challenged via a claim for [judicial] review – has resulted in the restriction of one of the claimant’s highly protected fundamental rights without constitutional grounds or a legal basis.

...

[58] The Kúria maintains its interpretation set forth in decision no. Kvk.IV.37.359/2014/2, according to which a violation of the requirement to exercise rights in accordance with their purpose does not follow from a mere finding of a legal infringement; there must be an obvious intent to exploit the substance of the legal institution in an unlawful manner under the guise of formal compliance with the law. According to the Kúria[‘s case-law], although a call to cast an invalid vote may run counter to the constitutional purpose of the referendum as a legal institution and to the spirit of the Initiating Referendums, European Citizens’ Initiative and Referendum Procedure Act and the [EPA], thereby potentially raising the issue of an exercise of rights contrary to their intended purpose, freedom of speech warrants special protection, even in the context of a referendum initiated by the Government, and its restriction would have been permissible only on constitutional and lawful grounds. Through their campaign activity, the claimant was exercising their fundamental right to freedom of expression, which cannot be lawfully restricted based on the grounds cited by the [NEC]. In the posts to which objection was raised, the claimant did not act abusively but rather – exercising its constitutional right – encouraged visitors to their social media page to cast invalid votes as an expression of their opinion on a matter of public interest; thus, they did not violate the fundamental principle of referendum procedure requiring the exercise of rights in good faith and in accordance with their intended purpose, as stipulated in section 2(1)(e) of the [EPA], as applicable pursuant to section 1(1) of the Initiating Referenda, European Citizens’ Initiative and Referendum Procedure Act.

...”

26.  Decision no. Kvk.V.39.422/2022/3 of the Kúria (see paragraph 21 above) contains the following relevant passages:

“...

[30] ... Under Article XXIII § 7 of the Fundamental Law, participation in a referendum is not an obligation for voters but a fundamental right; voters may exercise that right by abstaining from the referendum, or by participating and casting either a valid or an invalid vote. Casting an invalid vote does not constitute a violation of law; rather, it expresses the voter’s intent to refrain from making a substantive decision regarding the questions posed. The expression of opinion by the claimants participating in the referendum campaign – and their influencing of how voters exercise their right to participate in the referendum (in the manner described in the statement) – does not infringe upon essence of the referendum as a constitutional value under the Fundamental Law, nor does it impair the voting autonomy of the electorate, given that voters have a lawful means of exercising their referendum rights through abstention or by casting an invalid vote.

...

[32] ... The practice of the Constitutional Court is also consistent in finding that public communications (when the information shared is related to public life) are subject to enhanced fundamental-law protection. Decision 7/2014. (III. 7.) AB pointed out: ‘Freedom of speech requires special protection when it affects public affairs and the exercise of public power by persons performing public duties or taking part in public life. [Where] persons participating in the exercise of public power [are concerned], a restriction of freedom of expression would be justified in a much narrower range of cases under the constitutional requirements arising from the democratic rule of law.’ ...

...

[34] Regarding the requirement of exercising rights in accordance with their purpose, the [NEC] decision referred to the consistent judicial practice embodied in the Kúria’s decision no. Kvk.IV.37.359/2014/2. According to this practice, the requirement to exercise rights in accordance with their purpose – derived from civil law regulations prohibiting the abuse of rights – permeates the entire legal system. It implies that those entitled to exercise legal rights must do so in a manner consistent with the specific purpose and substance of those rights. Statutory protection and recognition are accorded only to the exercise of a right where its true substance is discernible beyond mere formal compliance with the rules governing that right. A violation of the requirement to exercise rights in accordance with their purpose goes beyond a mere finding of illegality; it must be an obvious intent to exploit the substance of the legal institution under the guise of formal compliance. In the present case, the Kúria has held that while a call to cast an invalid vote might conflict with the constitutional purpose of the referendum and the spirit of the relevant Acts (the Initiating Referenda, European Citizens’ Initiative and Referendum Procedure Act and the [EPA]), thereby potentially raising the issue of exercising a right contrary to its intended purpose, freedom of speech – specifically the expression of opinion on matters of public interest, including in the context of a referendum initiated by the Government – merits special protection; any restriction thereof is permissible only on the basis of the constitutional and legal grounds.

...

[37] ... Undoubtedly, the will of the people manifested through a referendum may be expressed not only by casting “yes” or “no” votes but also by a voter abstaining or – albeit with a different effect – casting an invalid vote. As the claimants rightly pointed out, the latter – as an expression of political opinion – constitutes a position that voters may adopt and articulate, regardless of the fact that its effect amounts to an exercise of rights contrary to their intended purpose. Indeed, there is no provision of law prohibiting a campaign message advocating the casting of an invalid vote. When assessing any restriction on political opinion, due regard must always be paid to the right to freedom of expression and the heightened constitutional protection afforded to political communication.

[38] The claimants correctly derived the primacy of freedom of expression from Article I § 3 of the Fundamental Law; freedom of expression holds a distinguished place among constitutional fundamental rights, and it cannot be curtailed simply by classifying a call to cast an invalid vote as an exercise of rights contrary to their intended purpose.

[39] Consequently, based on the arguments set forth in the claim for judicial review, no violation of section 2(1)(e) of the [EPA] could be established.

...”

27.  Decision no. Kvk.VI.39.423/2022/6 of the Kúria (see paragraph 23 above) contains the following relevant passages:

“...

[49] Constitutional Court decision no. 3313/2019 (XI. 21.) AB clearly stated that campaign activities not prohibited by the [EPA] are lawful, and that the fundamental principles of the [EPA] must also prevail during the campaign period. The aim of activities carried out during an election campaign is to influence, or attempt to influence, the will of the electorate. When assessing restrictions on campaign activities, due regard must always be given to the right to freedom of expression and the heightened constitutional protection afforded to political communication.

[50] The decision of the [NEC] does not state that the fundamental principle set out in section 2(1)(e) of the [EPA], or the provisions concerning election campaigns, restrict in any manner or to any extent the fundamental rights of participation in a national referendum and freedom of expression. In the absence of a statutory restriction – established and justified in detail by the NEC with reference to the provisions of the Fundamental Law – the expression of an opinion by the claimant during its campaign activity (a right guaranteed by the Fundamental Law) cannot be objected to.

[51] While the claimant’s campaign activity encouraged people to cast invalid votes, it did not affect the voters’ participation in the referendum or their voting autonomy. Voters remained free to decide, if they choose to exercise their right to participate, whether to vote ‘yes’ or ‘no’, or to deliberately cast an invalid vote.

[52] The [NEC] was required to evaluate the claimant’s campaign activity, not the result that emerged as a consequence of that activity. It had to assess the campaign activity independently, rather than in the light of the result.

[53] In decisions nos. Kvk.III.37.107/2008/2, Kvk.IV.37.468/2006/2 and KvkIII.37.211/2006/3, the Supreme Court, in accordance with Act C of 1997 on Electoral Procedure, established that a violation of the fundamental principle of exercising rights in good faith and for their intended purpose occurs when election participants exercise their election-related rights in a manner intended to mislead voters, by concealing or distorting facts, thereby diminishing the electoral prospects of their political opponents.

[54] In decisions nos. Kvk.IV.37.359/2014/2 and Kvk.I.37.394/2014/2, the Kúria, addressing the principle of exercising rights in good faith and in accordance with their purpose, found that the requirement to exercise rights for their intended purpose is one that permeates the entire legal system, including the rules of the [EPA]; this requirement derives from civil law regulations prohibiting the abuse of rights, dictating that the subjects of legal institutions may utilise them only in a manner consistent with their specific purpose and substance. Legal protection and recognition are only afforded to the exercise of a right when it reflects the true substance [and purpose of that right], beyond the formal requirements of the entitlement. A violation of the principle of exercising rights in accordance with their purpose goes beyond the mere establishment of an infringement: it must clearly manifest an intent to exploit the substance of a legal institution while ostensibly complying with the law.

[55] The claimant’s campaign activity, as established by the [NEC], could not have infringed upon freedom of expression, given the absence of statutory restrictions on the relevant Fundamental Law provisions; nor did it involve any intentional violation aimed at curtailing the will of the electorate or misleading voters; consequently, no violation of the fundamental principles of good faith and the exercise of rights in accordance with their purpose could be established.

...”
target_issue: Freedom of expression; Freedom to impart information; Freedom to receive ideas
target_question: whether the Court finds a violation by Hungary of Article 10 (Freedom of expression) concerning Freedom of expression; Freedom to impart information; Freedom to receive ideas in this case

case_name: CASE OF TAŞ v. TÜRKİYE
full_case_text_no_verdict:
SECOND SECTION

CASE OF TAŞ v. TÜRKİYE

(Application no. 40838/23)













JUDGMENT


STRASBOURG

3 November 2026



This judgment is final but it may be subject to editorial revision.

In the case of Taş v. Türkiye,

The European Court of Human Rights (Second Section), sitting as a Committee composed of:

Jovan Ilievski, President,
Gediminas Sagatys,
Hugh Mercer, judges,
and Dorothee von Arnim, Deputy Section Registrar,

Having regard to:

the application (no. 40838/23) against the Republic of Türkiye lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) on 9 November 2023 by a Turkish national, Mr Ersan Taş (“the applicant”), who was born in 1984, lives in Istanbul and was represented by Mr K. Altıparmak, a lawyer practising in Ankara;

the decision to give notice of complaint concerning Article 10 of the Convention to the Turkish Government (“the Government”), represented by their Agent, Mr Abdullah Aydın, Head of the Department of Human Rights of the Ministry of Justice of the Republic of Türkiye, and to declare inadmissible the remainder of the application;

the parties’ observations;

the decision to dismiss the Government’s objection to the examination of the application by a Committee;

Having deliberated in private on 6 October 2026,

Delivers the following judgment, which was adopted on that date:

SUBJECT MATTER OF THE CASE

1.  The application concerns a prison sentence combined with a measure of suspension of the pronouncement of the judgment, imposed on the applicant following his criminal conviction for the offences of insulting the President of the Republic and insulting a public official.

2.  At the time of the events in question the applicant was the holder of an account on the social media platform then called Twitter. The applicant’s account, named “@06melihchina”, was followed by more than 55,000 users of the platform. It was a parody account that portrayed jokes concerning the then mayor of Ankara, İ.M.G.

3.  On 24 September 2014 the official account of İ.M.G. on the same platform posted a photo and a mocking statement in respect of the then chairman of the main opposition party, K.K. On the same day, the applicant made a comment under that post. The applicant’s comment included a derisive image pertaining to the President and İ.M.G. accompanied by the following statement: “We continue to work and steal tirelessly with our President, God willing” (Cumhurbaşkanımızla birlikte hiç durmadan çalışmaya ve çalmaya devam ediyoruz Allah’ın izniyle).

4.  On 17 December 2014 İ.M.G filed a criminal complaint against the applicant on account of the content of his comment.

5.  On 26 September 2017 the Ankara Criminal Court of First Instance (hereinafter “the Criminal Court”) sentenced the applicant to eleven months and twenty days’ and ten months’ imprisonment for insulting the President of the Republic and insulting a public official on account of his functions, respectively. It decided, however, to suspend the pronouncement of the judgment under Article 231 § 5 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (see, for the text of this provision at the material time, Durukan and Birol v. Türkiye, nos. 14879/20 and 13440/21, § 23, 3 October 2023) and to apply a five‑year supervision period.

6.  On 9 November 2017 the Ankara Assize Court dismissed the objection lodged by the applicant against that decision, finding that it had been made in accordance with both procedural and substantial law.

7.  On 20 December 2017 the applicant lodged an individual application with the Constitutional Court. Relying on Article 10 of the Convention, he complained, inter alia, about his conviction owing to the comment in question.

8.  On 29 March 2023 the Constitutional Court found a violation of the applicant’s right to freedom of expression, in a judgment grouping similar applications, in accordance with its findings in its Atilla Yazar and Others judgment (see, for detailed information regarding that judgment, Durukan and Birol, cited above, §§ 28-31).

9.  To redress the violation, the Constitutional Court ordered a retrial and decided to send a copy of its judgment to the Criminal Court for the reopening of the criminal proceedings. Moreover, it ordered the reimbursement of the court fees paid by the applicant before the Criminal Court, as well as his legal representation costs. However, it rejected the applicant’s just satisfaction claims in respect of non-pecuniary damage. The decision was served on the applicant’s lawyer on 13 July 2023.

10.  On 9 November 2023 the applicant introduced his application before the Court.

11.  On the same day, the applicant lodged a petition with the Criminal Court seeking a retrial in order to secure the implementation of the Constitutional Court’s judgment.

12.  On 12 December 2023 the Criminal Court rejected the applicant’s request with a final decision, stating that the Constitutional Court had not yet delivered its decision concerning the applicant’s individual application.

13.  On 15 November 2024 the Constitutional Court filed a petition with the Criminal Court requesting information on the retrial proceedings.

14.  On 21 November 2024 the Criminal Court informed the Constitutional Court that the retrial proceedings had not been commenced, without providing any reasons.

15.  In his application to the Court, relying on Article 10 of the Convention, the applicant complained that his right to freedom of expression had been breached on account of his conviction and prison sentence, combined with a measure of suspension of the pronouncement of the judgment, owing to a comment he had posted on social media.
target_question: whether the Court finds a violation by Türkiye of Article 10 (Freedom of expression) concerning Freedom of expression in this case

case_name: CASE OF A.M. v. BULGARIA
full_case_text_no_verdict:
FIFTH SECTION

CASE OF A.M. v. BULGARIA

(Application no. 23441/25)













JUDGMENT



STRASBOURG

5 November 2026



This judgment is final but may be subject to editorial revision.

In the case of A.M. v. Bulgaria,

The European Court of Human Rights (Fifth Section), sitting as a Committee composed of:

María Elósegui, President,
Gilberto Felici,
Diana Sârcu, judges,
and Sophie Piquet, Acting Deputy Section Registrar,

Having regard to:

the application (no. 23441/25) against the Republic of Bulgaria lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) on 1 August 2025 by an Uzbek national, A.M. (“the applicant”), who was born in 1981 and was represented by Mr V. Petkov, a lawyer practising in Sofia;

the decisions to indicate an interim measure to the Bulgarian Government (“the Government”) and to refuse to lift that measure;

the decision not to have the applicant’s full name disclosed;

the decision to give priority to the application;

the decision to give notice of the application to the Government, represented by their Agents, Ms M. Kotseva and Ms S. Sobadzhieva of the Ministry of Justice;

the parties’ observations;

Having deliberated in private on 15 October 2026,

Delivers the following judgment, which was adopted on that date:

SUBJECT MATTER OF THE CASE

1.  The applicant arrived in Bulgaria in August 2022 and applied for international protection in October 2022. The State Agency for Refugees (“the SAR”) interviewed him and, under an accelerated procedure, rejected his application as manifestly unfounded. The Sofia City Administrative Court (“the SCAC”) upheld that decision following a claim for judicial review lodged by the applicant.

2.  In December 2022 the applicant lodged a subsequent application for international protection, enclosing an opinion by a psychologist whom he had consulted. The SAR rejected that application without an examination on the merits. The applicant again sought judicial review, and the SCAC again upheld the SAR’s decision.

3.  In April 2023 the applicant lodged a second subsequent application for international protection, enclosing a report by two forensic medical experts who had examined him and four documents he described as having been issued by the Uzbek authorities. The SAR rejected that application without an examination on the merits, but the SCAC set that decision aside after the applicant lodged a claim for judicial review. After interviewing the applicant, the SAR dismissed the application. The SCAC upheld that decision, and the Supreme Administrative Court (“the SAC”) in turn upheld the SCAC’s judgment on appeal.

4.  In June 2025 the applicant lodged a third subsequent application for international protection. The SAR rejected it without considering it on the merits. The applicant sought judicial review of that decision, but subsequently withdrew his claim, whereupon the SCAC discontinued the relevant proceedings. He later stated that he wished to retract the withdrawal, and the SCAC directed him to clarify whether that statement was intended as an appeal against the discontinuance. The applicant took no steps to comply with that direction, and the discontinuance became final.

5.  Meanwhile, in February 2023, the migration authorities had ordered the applicant’s return to Uzbekistan. He sought judicial review of that order but the order was upheld by the SCAC. The SAC upheld the SCAC’s judgment on appeal. The applicant subsequently sought to have the proceedings before the SAC reopened but later abandoned that attempt.

6.  In July 2025 the applicant was placed in immigration detention. Separately, having twice attempted to cross the border into Romania illegally in March and April 2025, in October 2025 he was sentenced to eighteen months’ imprisonment.

7.  The applicant remained in prison, serving that sentence, until June 2026. He was then placed in immigration detention.

8.  The applicant complained under Article 3 of the Convention that the Bulgarian authorities and courts had not properly assessed whether he would be at a risk of ill-treatment if removed to Uzbekistan, and that, since that risk was real, such removal would be in breach of that Article.
target_question: whether the Court finds a violation by Bulgaria of Article 3 (Prohibition of torture) concerning Expulsion; Conditional; Uzbekistan in this case
